body.p: ACT I Alaska Commercial Company's Store at Dawson
ACT II Anteroom of Pioneer Hall
ACT III Freda Moloof's Cabin
Time of play, 1897, Dawson, Northwest Territory. It occurs in thirteen hours.
Freda Moloof............A dancer.
Floyd Vanderlip.........An Eldorado king.
Loraine Lisznayi........A Hungarian.
Captain Eppingwell......United States government agent.
Mrs. Eppingwell.........His wife.
Flossie.................Engaged to marry Floyd Vanderlip
Sitka Charley...........An Indian dog-driver.
Dave Harney.............An Eldorado king.
Prince..................A mining engineer.
Mrs. McFee..............Whose business is morals.
Minnie..................Maid to Freda Moloof.
Dog-punchers, couriers, miners, Indians, mounted police, clerks, etc.

FREDA MOLOOF. A Greek girl and a dancer. Speaks perfect English, but withal has that slight, indefinable foreign touch of accent. Good figure, willowy, yet not too slender. Of indeterminate age, possibly no more than twenty-five. Her furs the most magnificent in all the Yukon country from Chilcoot to St. Michael's, her name common on the lips of men.

FLOYD VANDERLIP. An Eldorado king, worth a couple of millions. Simple, elemental, almost childish in his emotions. But a brave man, and masculine; a man who has done a man's work in the world. Has caressed more shovel-handles than women's hands. Big-muscled, big-bodied, ingenuous-faced; the sort of a man whom women of the right sort can tie into knots.

LORAINE LISZNAYI. A Hungarian, reputed to be wealthy, and to be travelling in the Klondike for pleasure and love of adventure. Past the flush of youth, and with fair success feigning youth. In the first stages of putting flesh upon her erstwhile plumpness. Dark-eyed, a flashing, dazzling brunette, with a cosmopolitan reputation earned in a day when she posed in the studios of artist-queens and received at her door the cards of cardinals and princes.
CAPTAIN EPPINGWELL. Special agent for the United States government.

MRS. EPPINGWELL. His wife. Twenty-five to twenty-eight years of age. Of the cold order of women, possessing sanity, and restraint, and control. Brown hair, demi-blond type, oval-faced, with cameo-like features. The kind of a woman who is not painfully good, but who acts upon principle and who knows always just what she is doing.
FLOSSIE. Eighteen or nineteen years of age. Of the soft and clinging kind, with pretty, pouting lips, blow-away hair, and eyes full of the merry shallows of life. Engaged to marry Floyd Vanderlip.
PRINCE. A young mining engineer. A good fellow, a man's man.
MRS. MCFEE. Near to forty, Scotch accent, sharp-featured, and unbeautiful, with an eager nose that leads her into the affairs of others. So painfully good that it hurts.

SITKA CHARLEY. An Indian dog-puncher, who has come into the warm and sat by the fires of the white man until he is somewhat as one of them. Should not be much shorter than Vanderlip and Captain Eppingwell.
DAVE HARNEY. An Eldorado king, also a Yankee, with a fondness for sugar and a faculty for sharp dealing. Is tall, lean, loose-jointed. Walks with a shambling gait. Speaks slowly, with a drawl.
MINNIE. (Maid to Freda.) A cool, impassive young woman.
POLICEMAN. A young fellow, with small blond mustache. An Englishman, brave, cool, but easily embarrassed. Though he says "Sorry" frequently, he is never for an instant afraid.
ACT I—ALASKA COMPANY'S STORE AT DAWSON
ACT II—ANTEROOM OF PIONEER HALL
ACT III—FREDA MOLOOF'S CABIN

div.head: Scorn of Women: A Play In Three Acts
ACT I—ALASKA COMPANY'S STORE AT DAWSON
div.p: Scene. Alaska Commercial Company's store at Dawson. It is eleven o'clock of a cold winter morning. In front, on the left, a very large wood-burning stove. Beside the stove is a woodbox filled with firewood. Farther back, on left, a door with sign on it, "Private." On right, door, a street entrance; alongside are wisp-brooms for brushing snow from moccasins. In the background a long counter running full length of room with just space at either end for ingress or egress. Large gold-scales rest upon counter. Behind counter equally long rows of shelves, broken in two places by ordinary small-paned house-windows. Windows are source of a dim, gray light. Doors, window-frames, and sashes are of rough, unstained pine boards. Shelves practically empty, with here and there upon them an article of hardware (such as pots, pans, and tea-kettles), or of dry-goods (such as pasteboard boxes and bolts of cloth). The walls of the store are of logs stuffed between with brown moss. On counter, furs, moccasins, mittens, and blankets, piled up or spread out for inspection. In front of counter many snow-shoes, picks, shovels, axes, gold-pans, axe-handles, and oblong sheet-iron Yukon stoves. The feature most notable is the absence of foodstuffs in any considerable quantity. On shelves a few tins of mushrooms, a few bottles of olives.

About the stove, backs to the stove and hands behind their backs, clad in mackinaw suits, mittens dangling from around their necks at ends of leather thongs, ear-flaps of fur caps raised, are several miners. Prince stands by stove An Indian is replenishing the fire with great chunks of wood. Mounted police pass in and out. Sitka Charley is examining snow-shoes, bending and testing them. Behind the counter are several clerks, one of whom is waiting upon a bearded miner near end of counter to right.

div.head: MINER
div.p: (Pathetically.) No flour?

div.head: MINER
div.p: No beans?

div.head: MINER
div.p: No sugar?

div.head: CLERK

p.hi: (Coming from behind counter and approaching stove, visibly irritated, shaking his head violently; midway he encounters Miner, who retreats backward before him.)

div.p: No! No! No! I tell you no! No flour, no beans, no sugar, nothing!

p.hi: (Warms his hands over stove and glares ferociously at Miner.)

(Dave Harney enters from right, brushes snow from moccasins, and walks across to stove. He is tall and lean, has a loose-jointed, shambling gait, and listens interestedly to Clerk and Miner. He evinces a desire to speak, but his mustached mouth is so iced-up that he cannot open it. He bends over stove to thaw the ice.)

div.head: MINER
div.p: It's all very well for your playing the high an' lofty, you sneakin' little counter-jumper. But we all know what your damned Company is up to. You're holdin' grub for a rise, that's what you're doin'. Famine prices is your game.

div.head: CLERK
div.p: Look at the shelves, man! Look at them!

div.head: MINER
div.p: How about the warehouses, eh? Stacked to the roof with grub!

div.head: CLERK
div.p: They're not.

div.head: MINER
div.p: I suppose you'll say they're empty.

div.head: CLERK
div.p: They're not. But what little grub's in them belongs to the sour-doughs who filed their orders last spring and summer before ever you thought of coming into the country. And even the sourdoughs are scaled down, cut clean in half. Now shut up. I don't want to hear any more from you. You newcomers needn't think you're going to run this country, because you ain't.
Damned cheechawker!

div.head: MINER

p.hi: (Breaking down and showing fear, not of Clerk, but of famine.)

div.p: But good heavens, man, what am I to do? I haven't fifty pounds of flour for the whole winter.
I can pay for my grub if you'll sell it to me. You can't leave me starve!

div.head: DAVE HARNEY

p.hi: (Tearing the last chunk oj ice from mustache and sending it rattling to the floor. He speaks with a drawl.)

div.p: Aw, you tenderfeet make me tired. I never seen the beat of you critters. Better men than you have starved in this country, an' they didn't make no bones about it neither—they was all bones I calkilate. What do you think this is? A Sunday picnic? Jes' come in, eh? An' you're clean scairt. Look at me—old-timer, sir, a sour-dough, an' proud of it! I come into this country before there was any blamed Company, fished for my breakfast, an' hunted my supper. An' when the fish didn't bite an' they wa'n't any game, jes' cinched my belt tighter an' hiked along, livin' on salmon-bellies and rabbit tracks an' eatin' my moccasins.
Oh, I tell you this is the country that'll take the saleratus out of you!

p.hi: (Miner, awed by being face to face with an old-timer, withers up during harangue, and at finish shrinks behind other miners, and from there makes exit to right.)
(Drawing paper from pocket and presenting it.)

div.p: Now lookee here, Mister Clerk, what'd you call that?

div.head: CLERK
div.p: Grub contract.

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: What's it stand for?

div.head: CLERK
div.p: One thousand pounds of grub.

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: An' how much sugar?

div.head: CLERK
div.p: One thousand pounds of grub.

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: Say it again.

div.head: CLERK
div.p: (Looking for item on paper and reading.) Seventy-five pounds.

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: That's the way I made it out. I thought my eyes was all right.

div.head: CLERK
div.p: Well?

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: Well, that mangy little cuss around at the warehouse said I could only get five hundred on that piece of paper, an' nary sugar. What's that mean?

div.head: CLERK
div.p: It means five hundred pounds and no sugar. Scale-down went into effect to-day. Orders.

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: An' nary sugar?

div.head: CLERK
div.p: Nary sugar.

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: That grub's mine, an' that sugar. I paid for it last spring. Weighed my dust in on them scales there.

div.head: CLERK
div.p: Can't help it. Orders.

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: An' nary sugar?

div.head: CLERK
div.p: Nary sugar.

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: Curious, ain't it? Mighty curious—me ownin' two five-hundred-foot Eldorado claims, with five million if I'm wuth a cent, an' no sweetenin' for my coffee or mush.

p.hi: ('Whirling upon Clerk in sudden wrath, Clerk retreating wearily to behind counter.)

div.p: Why, gosh dang it! this country kin go to blazes! I'll sell out! I'll quit it cold! I'll—I'll—go back to the States! I'll—I'll—see the management!

div.head: CLERK
div.p: Hold on!
The boss is busy. Vanderlip's with'm.

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: He's buckin' the sugar proposition, too, eh? Clerk
No, he ain't.

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: Then here goes. Dave Harney don't wait on Vanderlip or any other man.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Hello, Dave. What's the rush?

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: Hello, Vanderlip. Got any sugar to sell?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: No, but I want to buy—

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: No sugar, you can't do business with me.

p.hi: (Rushes through door, slamming it after him.)
(General laugh from miners about stove. Clerk throws up his arms despairingly.)
(Vanderlip looks backward through door, which he pulls open for a moment, and laughs at Dave Harney.)
(Loraine Lisznayi enters from right and pauses at door to brush snow from moccasins.)

div.head: VANDERLIP

p.hi: (Sees Loraine Lisznayi, starts across to meet her, but stops midway to speak hurriedly to Sitka Charley.)

div.p: How about those dogs, Charley?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: I get um all right by and by.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: I want them right away, to-day.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Yesterday you tell me to-morrow.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: To-day, I tell you to-day. Never mind the price. I must have them—good dogs. Tonight, twelve o'clock, have them down at the water-hole all ready, harnesses, grub, everything in shape. And you're to drive them down river for me. Sure?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Sure.

div.head: VANDERLIP

p.hi: (Over his shoulder as he continues to cross to right.)

div.p: Never mind the price. I must have them.

p.hi: (Crosses on over to right to Loraine Lisznayi, an expression of joy on his face. Sweeps off his Fur cap and shakes her hand.)

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: You must do better than that. Had there been a woman here, your face would have given everything away.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: I can't help the gladness getting into my face, Loraine.

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: Don't call me Loraine. Somebody might hear. And we can't be too careful. And you mustn't talk but for a moment, Floyd.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: There you go, calling me Floyd. Somebody might hear. But who's afraid? I'm not. Let 'em hear. I'm glad of it! Proud of it that you're mine. The dearest little woman in the world, and mine, all mine!

div.head: LORAINE

p.hi: (Glancing furtively about and finding that nobody is paying any attention.)

div.p: Hush, dear. Wait until we are safely away, and then I shall be proud before all the world to have you proud of me. You are such a man! Such a man!

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Just wait until I get you into that Mediterranean palace. We'll make 'em sit up with this Klondike gold of ours. People don't know how rich I am, Loraine. Nor do you. I've got pay-claims over on Dominion Creek nobody dreams of, and—

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: I don't care how much you've got, or how little. It's you, you big, big man, you, my hero, that I care for. You'll grace a palace like a prince, and I've known a few princes, too.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: And queens, too, didn't you say?

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: Yes, and queens, too. And they will be proud and glad to know you. They don't have men like you over there—real men. You'll create a sensation.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: But this living in palaces—sort of softening and fattening, ain't it? I don't like fat.
You don't incline that way, do you?

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: You foolish, dear man, of course not. Do I look it?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Well, you look round—and plump.

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: I've always been plump like this. I'm like my mother. She was that way. She never got stout, and neither shall I.

div.head: VANDERLIP

p.hi: (Anxiety going out of face, being replaced by satisfaction.)

div.p: Oh, you're all right, Loraine, you bet.

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: But you must leave me now, Floyd. Somebody may come in at any moment. Besides, I've a few little things to buy for our journey.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: And they're fixing my money for me in there.

(Nodding toward door at lejt. Loraine betrays keen and involuntary interest). Letters of credit, you know, and all that. Can't carry much dust. Too heavy. And by the way, keep the weight down. Don't buy too many little things. Dogs are dogs, and they can only haul so much.

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: Only enough for me to be comfortable.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: A woman needs so almighty much to be comfortable. But it'll be all right. Two sleds'll carry us, no matter how comfortable you make yourself. Bring plenty of foot-gear, moccasins, and stockings, and such things. And be at the water-hole at midnight with your whole outfit. Be sure that Indian of yours has enough dog food. I'll get my dogs to-day some time.

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: Which water-hole?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: The one by the hospital. Don't make a mistake and go to the other one. It's way out of the way.

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: And now you simply must leave me. And you mustn't see me again to-day—not till midnight, at the water-hole, by the hospital. You know I can scarcely bear to have you out of my sight. But these women—oh, they are such suspicious creatures!

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Good-by, then, until to-night.

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: Floyd!
You must go to the ball to-night. I've begged off, but you must go. It will avert any possible suspicion.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: I was going anyway, just to drop in for a while. I—that is, you see—I promised Mrs. Eppingwell I'd go.

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: (Jealously.) Mrs. Eppingwell!

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Of course, but it's all right, Loraine. She don't count.

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: Of course not. But then, Floyd, I care so much for you that I can't help a little jealousy—but there, there, you must go. Good-by, dear.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Good-by dear, dear Loraine. (Turns to go toward left.)

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: (Softly.) Floyd!

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: (Turns back, waits, and after a pause.) Well?

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: I've been hearing things about you, sir.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: What's up now?

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: Oh, you seem to have—how shall I say!—a penchant for foreigners.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Darned if I know what you're talking about. Penchant—is that something to eat?

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: Well, then, there is a certain woman, supposed to be Greek, at any rate a foreigner like myself; but with the most adorable accent—or so the men say—

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Freda, you mean.

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: Yes, I believe that is the woman's name.
Vanderlip (Laughing jovially.)
There ain't anything in it. I don't care a rap for her—not a rap.

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: Then there's that Mrs. Eppingwell. I can't help thinking you are a little devoted to her.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Oh, well, I've only seen her in a social way—that's all, in a social way.

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: And you do love only me?
Then tell me that you do.

div.head: VANDERLIP

p.hi: (With impulsive eagerness, half lifting his arms as if to embrace her and controlling himself with an effort.)

div.p: Oh, I do, Loraine. I do, I do.

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: It is sweet to hear you say it. And now you really must go. Good-by, dear, good-by.

p.hi: (He crosses stage to left and goes out.)
(She starts to cross stage to rear, but is approached and stopped by Sitka Charley.)

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: (Gruffly.) Good morning.

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: Good morning, Charley.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: You got my money?

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: Oh, let me see. How much is it?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Two hundred dollar.

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: I'll tell you. You come to my cabin to-morrow morning, and I'll give it to you.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: (Not letting on that he knows she is lying.) To-morrow morning you give me money?

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: At my cabin, don't forget.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: All right, to-morrow morning.

p.hi: (He turns abruptly and starts to go toward stove.)

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: Oh, Charley!
Is Dominion Creek very rich?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Dam rich.

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: And do you know whether Mr. Vanderlip has any claims there?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Me no know.

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: But Mr. Vanderlip is very rich, isn't he? You know that?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Vanderlip dam rich.

p.hi: (Sitka Charley turns abruptly and goes back to stove.)
(Loraine crosses stage to left rear to counter, where a clerk waits upon her.)
(Enter Mrs. Eppingwell and Mrs. McFee from right. Both engage in brushing snow from moccasins.)

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: (Finishing first, and looking about the store as if in quest of some one.) as I don't see anything of Captain Eppingwell, and he is the soul of promptness.
MRS. McFEE

Mayhap we are a bit early, Mrs. Eppingwell. But as I was saying, it's verra dootful morals the giving of this masked ball. Masked, mind you, with every low dance-hall creature a-dying to come and put decent folk to the shame of their company. I speak my mind, and it's ay shameful that honest bodies must be so sore put. There'll be ruffians and gamblers with masks over their sinful faces, and who's to know? And there's that Freda woman. 'Tis said she plays with the souls of men as a child with a wee bit of a pipe plays with soap-bubbles. And there's all the rest—bold hussies!—who's to stop them from flaunting their fine feathers in our faces? Who's to stop them, I make free to ask?

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: The doorkeeper, of course. It is quite simple. Masks must be lifted at the door.
MRS. McFEE
Ou, ay, verra simple, I should say. Belike you'll undertake the doorkeeping, and belike you'll know the face of every rapscallion of them.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: We'll get one of the men who do know—Mr. Prince, for example. There he is, by the stove. We'll ask him to be doorkeeper.

p.hi: (Prince goes to rear and joins Loraine.)

div.p: MRS. McFEE
And how comes it Mr. Prince should know the children of sin and still be company for decent bodies?

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Because he is a man, I imagine.
There is Sitka Charley. I suppose you would bar him if he wanted to come?

div.head: MRS. MCFEE
div.p: Why, no, he's a verra good soul.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Yet I'm sure he knows all the children of sin, you call them.
MRS. McFEE
But he's an Indian, and he doesna dance.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Then I suppose I shall not shock you by speaking to him.

p.hi: (Approaches Sitka Charley, while Mrs. McFee goes to counter and is waited on by a clerk.)

div.p: Good morning, Charley. Have you seen Captain Eppingwell?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Yes.
Mrs. Eppingwell How long ago? Was he here?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: I see um last night.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Oh!
I've seen him later than that. But he was to meet me here.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: It is rather cold this morning.
Um.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: How cold?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Sixty-five below. Any dogs to sell?

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Still trying to buy dogs! For whom this time? Sitka Charley
Vanderlip. He want eight dogs.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: (Startled and interested.) Mr. Vanderlip?
Um.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Mrs. Eppingwell What does he want with dogs?
Sitka Charley Um. Got dogs?

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Yes, I've dogs to sell. Or rather, Captain Eppingwell has.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Fresh dogs? Strong dogs?

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Well, no. You see, he just arrived yesterday. It was a long trip.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Yes, me know—sixteen hundred miles. Dogs all bones, all played out, no good.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: How soon does he want the dogs?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Right away, now, to-day.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: What does he want the dogs for?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um?

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: What does Mr. Vanderlip want the dogs for?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: That no Sitka Charley's business. That Vanderlip's business.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: But I want to know.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Then you ask Vanderlip.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Tell me.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Much better you ask Vanderlip, I think so.

p.hi: (A pause, during which Sitka Charley merely waits, while Mrs. Eppingwell seems to be thinking. When she speaks, it is in a changed, serious tone.)

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Charley, we have travelled the Long Trail together, you and I.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: We journeyed through the Hills of Silence. We saw our last dogs drop in the traces. We staggered and fell, and crawled on our hands and knees through the snow because we had not enough to eat, and it was very cold. We had our last food stolen—

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY

p.hi: (Eyes flashing, face stiffening, grimly and with satisfaction.)

div.p: Captain Eppingwell kill one man who steal food. I kill other man. I know.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Yes, it was terrible. But we kept the faith of food and blanket, you and I, Charley.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: And Captain Eppingwell.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: And Captain Eppingwell. And by that faith of food and blanket I want you to tell me the truth now.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Will you?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Mr. Vanderlip wants dogs, fresh dogs—why? Sitka Charley
He make a long travel, many sleeps.
Mrs. Eppingwell Where? When? Tell me all.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um travel down river. Um start to-night.
Mrs. Eppingwell He goes alone?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: No.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Who goes with him?
Me go.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Yes, yes, of course. But you don't count. Anybody else?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Just as I thought. Tell me, Charley, it is—it is this—er—this horrid woman? You know.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um, this bad woman—this damn bad woman. Um, she go with him, to-night, twelve o'clock, the water-hole. She meet um there.
Mrs. Eppingwell (Eagerly.)
Yes, yes. And then....

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: And then she go with um, many sleeps, down the river.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: And you will get the dogs?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Sure, I get um.
(Enter Dave Harney from left, striding angrily.) I get um now—

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: Good-by.

p.hi: (Starts in the direction of Dave Harney.)

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Wait a minute, Charley.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: I come back. You wait.
Hello, Dave. Cold to-day.

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: You betcher life it's cold—regular freeze-out, with me frozen. But I'm goin' to quit it, quit it cold. I'll harness up my dogs and hit the high places for a land of justice where a man can get what he's ordered a year before and paid for.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Got any dogs to sell?

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: Got any sugar to sell?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: I buy um dogs.

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: I'm buyin' sugar.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: I got no sugar. You got dogs. I buy dogs eight dogs—how much?
Dave Harney Five hundred dollars a dog.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um—eight dogs—four thousand dollar.

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: Dogs is wuth what you're willin' to pay for 'em.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um.

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: Look here, Charley, I used to be a miner, but I'm a business man now. Got any sugar?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: No sugar.

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: I'll throw a lot off them dogs for some sugar. No sugar, they cost you four thousand.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um.

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: Four thousand,

div.head: CHARLEY
div.p: Um.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: They're wuth it if you want 'em real bad.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: All right, Dave. I buy.

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: Bring the dust around to my cabin at one o'clock.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: I buy now.

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: No, you don't. I'm goin' back to tell 'em what I think of 'em, the skunks! They've got sweetenin' in plenty for their own mush and coffee. You betcher life they have, and I'm goin' to get some of it or know the reason why.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: That Dave Harney all the same one big robber. But I get um dogs all right.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Tell me about this—er—this woman, Charley, this Freda—Freda Moloof her name is, isn't it?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY

p.hi: (Showing plainly that his attention has been called off from the consideration of Loraine Lisznayi.)

div.p: Oh, Freda!

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: You call her Freda.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Everybody call her Freda. Um good name. Me like it.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Well, what kind of a woman is she?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um good woman.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL

p.hi: (With an angry movement of arm and clenching of hand.)

div.p: Oh!

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: (Looking surprised and getting stubborn.) Me know Freda long time—two years. Um good woman. Um tongue speak true. Um just like you, no afraid. Um just like you, travel Long Trail with me. No afraid, very soft heart; sorry for dogs; no ride on sled when dogs tired. Um tired, but um walk. And um tongue straight; all the time speak true. I am Sitka Charley—I know.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Yes, yes. Go on.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Freda no like men.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Now that is too much, Charley? How about Mr. Vanderlip?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: I know Freda long time. Freda know Vanderlip short time. Maybe Freda like Vanderlip. I don't know. But before she never like men, that I know. Maybe you like Mr. Vanderlip I think. (Mrs. Eppingwell smiles, and Sitka Charley grows more positive.) Vanderlip come your cabin all the time. You ride on Vanderlip's sled. I know. I see. Maybe you like Vanderlip.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: You don't understand, Charley. I have reasons for being nice to Mr. Vanderlip.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: And, Charley, you mustn't tell anybody what you have told me about Mr. Vanderlip going away to-night with that—that woman.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Maybe I tell Freda.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Don't be foolish, Charley. She is the last person in the world who ought to know. Of course you'll not tell her. Tell no one.
Promise me you'll not tell. Promise me by the faith of food and blanket.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: All right, I no tell.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: They say Freda is a dancer. Have you seen her dance?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY

p.hi: (Nodding his heady a pleased expression on his face.)

div.p: I see um. Very good dance. Um dance at Juneau, two years ago, first time I see. Treadwell Mine no work that day. No men to work. All men come Juneau and look see Freda dance. Freda makum much money. Um speak to me. Um say, "Charley, I go Yukon Country. You drive my dogs, how much?" Then Freda travel Long Trail with me.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: They say many men like her.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um, sure. Me like her too, very much.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: And they say she makes fools of men.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Sure. Dam fools. Men just like bubble. Freda just make play with um—smash!—just like that. Everybody say so.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: What kind of a looking woman is she?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: You no see um?
Mrs. Eppingwell No. What does she look like?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um there now.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: What?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um Freda there.

p.hi: (Mrs. Eppingwell turns involuntarily to look. Freda pauses on entering, starts as though to retreat at sight of the crowd, then stiffens herself, face and body, to meet it, and proceeds to brush snow from moccasins. There is silence in store. Then a perturbation amongst miners about stove, men craning their heads over one another's shoulders to look at Freda. The clerks look at her. Everybody looks at her.)
(Mrs. McFee turns up her nose several degrees, and, plainly advertising a highly moral rage, walks over to Mrs. Eppingwell.)

div.p: MRS. McFEE

p.hi: (To Mrs. Eppingwell, but glaring at Freda.)

div.p: It's my way of thinking that it is high time for decent bodies to be going.

p.hi: (Sitka Charley glares angrily at Mrs. McFee.)

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Hush. It is a public place, and she has as much right here as you or I. Don't insult the poor woman.
MRS. McFEE
In my way of thinking the insult's the other way around. Come you, Mrs. Eppingwell, we must go. The verra air is contameenated.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Do please restrain yourself, Mrs. McFee. Don't make a scene.

div.head: MRS. MCFEE
div.p: I'll no restrain myself, and I'll no wait for you if you see proper no to come now. The hussy!

p.hi: (Mrs. McFee, nose high in the air, turns to make exit at right. Freda has just finished brushing snow, and has risen erect. Mrs. McFee, passing her to go out the door, sniffs audibly and draws aside her skirt. Freda makes no movement, though her lips tighten. Exit Mrs. McFee. Freda tries to hang up wisp-broom, but her hand trembles, misses peg, and wisp-broom falls to floor. She picks it up and this time hangs it properly. Turns and goes to right rear to counter, where clerk waits upon her.)

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: (Glaring after Mrs. McFee, angrily).
That womans no like Freda. What for?

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: No women like Freda.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: You no like Freda?

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: No, Charley, I do not like Freda.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: What for you no like Freda?

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: I cannot explain. You would not understand.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Me Sitka Charley. Me understand. What for you no like Freda?

div.head: I—
div.p: (Catching sight of Capt. Eppingwell.) There is Captain Eppingwell now.

p.hi: (Capt. Eppingwell brushes moccasins quickly, and goes immediately to Mrs. Eppingwell. Sitka Charley, still angry, joins group about stove.)

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Early, as usual, Maud.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: No, merely on time. It is you who are late. Capt. Eppingwell
Impossible!

p.hi: (Looks at his watch and smiles triumphantly.)

div.p: I knew it. On time to the tick of the second.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Not by Dawson time.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Oh! of course. I haven't changed my watch. I'm still going by sun-time. Sorry.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: I forgive you. It is the first time, but I really can't count it against you.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: What's wrong?

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Archie, you're the dearest man I know. Of course there is something wrong, and of course you knew it as soon as you set eyes on me. Well, I am beaten.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: The Ever-Victorious-One beaten! Impossible! I'll not believe it.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: I am, just the same. Here I have been trying to save Floyd Vanderlip, counteracting that evil woman's influence, having him to tea and dinner and giving him no end of my time, and Flossie isn't here yet, and he runs away with Freda Mo-loof to-night. It's all arranged, and everything.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: But—but—wait a minute. Enlighten me. I am only a poor traveller. Who is this Flossie? And why shouldn't this Vanderlip-man—whoever he is—run away if he wants to?

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: How ridiculous of me! I forget you've been away. You know who Freda Moloof is?

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Surely, surely. She has the most magnificent furs and the most magnificent dogs in all Alaska. A fascinating creature, I—er—understand. She plays with men as a child plays with bubbles.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: It seems to me I've heard that before.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: It has become a saying in the country.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: I have heard of men who whistle women up as they would whistle dogs. She must be the type of woman that whistles men.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: All she has to do is look at a man.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: You speak as though she had looked at you.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: A very interesting woman.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Well, anyway, she has cast eyes and wiles upon Floyd Vanderlip.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: But why shouldn't she? This is a free country.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Wait a minute. I'm trying to explain. Floyd Vanderlip is engaged to marry some one else.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: O-o-h!

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Floyd Vanderlip is a big, strong man. For five years he chased Eldorados over the ice-fields, living on moose and salmon and working like a beast. He never had an idle moment in which to be wicked. Then he struck it on Klondike and is worth millions and millions. Also, he sat down for the first time in five years and rested.

He remembered a girl who was waiting for him down in the States—a young thing—and sent for her to come in. They were to be married as soon as she arrived. He has a cabin all ready. Well, that's Flossie. She is coming in over the ice now—he's told me all about it—and ought to be here any day. I've been looking for her, and looking for her, till I am almost sick. Then this Freda Moloof cast her spell upon him. I heard the gossip—

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: And proceeded to take a hand. I begin to understand.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: I did my best to break her influence. The time and thought I've wasted upon that man! It's almost scandalous the way I've devoted myself to him! Sitka Charley believes I am in love with him—told me so to my face. And it's all wasted, card parties and everything. What was I against the only woman in Klondike who possesses a piano and a maid? And to-night he runs away down the river with her.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: With Freda Moloof?

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: With Freda Moloof. There she is now, buying things for the journey most probably.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL

p.hi: (Turning to look at Freda, and turning back again.)

div.p: I must say she couldn't have done better if he is worth all you say he is. I remember him now, a strapping fellow, brave as a lion and all that.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Yes, but he's caressed more shovel-handles than women's hands, and that's the trouble with him. And I don't know what I shall do.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: You could scarcely serve an injunction on him.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: I don't know what I'll do. Floyd Vanderlip is not the sort of man to appeal to. To try to impress him to do the right thing would be like setting fire to a powder mill. I wish I knew how near Flossie is. There hasn't been a courier or a mail carrier in for weeks and weeks. The mail from Dyea is twenty days overdue.

p.hi: (Enter Mail Carrier, carrying leather mail-pouch. He is clad in a long squirrel-skin parka reaching to his knees, the hood drawn over his head and ears and leaving only jace exposed. Face and mouth are iced-up, making speech impossible. He does not stop to brush snow jrom moccasins, but proceeds rapidly to cross to stove.)

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: There is the man who can tell you about Flossie. Shall I ask him?

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Oh! the mail carrier? At last! And in the nick of time. Yes, do.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL

p.hi: (Stepping into the path of the Mail Carrier.)

div.p: What's the news?

p.hi: (Mail Carrier makes dumb show that he cannot speak, waving his arms and pointing to his iced mouth and then to the stove.)
(Capt. Eppingwell laughs and lets him pass.)

div.p: He's so iced up he cannot speak. Wait till he thaws out, and then I'll get hold of him. In the meantime—

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: In the meantime you must meet the Lisznayi.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: The Lisznayi!

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Yes, she is a fascinating woman, our latest acquisition. An Old World Hungarian with all the do and dare of the New World blood. She was a friend of the Queen of Roumania. Posed as a model for the Queen. Had cardinals and princes at her beck and call. Plenty of money, of course, position, and all that. Came into the Klondike out of sheer love of adventure, and possibly because she was bored. You'll enjoy her, I know. There she is over there. Do you care to?

p.hi: (Mrs. Eppingwell and Capt. Eppingwell walk over to left rear to Loraine Lisznayi and Prince.)

(Mail Carrier tries to get to stove, but is blocked by miners, who are demanding: "What's the news?" "How's the trail?" "Any letters for me?" "And me?" "And me?" "Where did you meet O'Brien? He left ten days ago." "How's the ice on Thirty Mile River?" etc.y etc. To all of which Mail Carrier replies by waving his arms and thrusting through the crowd till he gets to stove, over which he holds his Face.)

(Dave Harney enters from left, still in towering rage, but his jace lights up, as though struck by a sudden thought when he catches sight oj Mail Carrier. He strides over, clutches Mail Carrier by the arm and draws him to one side.)

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: Got a noospaper?

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: How many?

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: I'll give you twenty dollars for it.

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: (Bidding rapidly, each bid being met by a shake of Mail Carrier's head.) Twenty-five. Thirty. Thirty-five. Forty. Fifty.

p.hi: (Nods head and goes back to stove.)
(Freda walks forward toward stove and beckons to Sitka Charley, who leaves group about stove and comes to her.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Tell the Mail Carrier I want to speak to him, Charley.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Urn.

p.hi: (Sitka Charley crosses to stove, where Mail Carrier is pulling the ice from his mouth.)

div.p: Freda want talk some with you.

div.head: MAIL CARRIER

p.hi: (Turning to look at Freda, nods head and mumbles incoherently, at same time starting to go to Freda and still pulling ice jrom mouth. He shakes hands with Freda and speaks thickly at first.)

div.p: How do do, Freda.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: How do you do, Joe. What kind of a trip did you have?

div.head: MAIL CARRIER
div.p: Pretty rough, but I made good time just the same. Passed everything in sight.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: That is what I wanted to ask you about. Did you pass the outfit of a girl, or, rather, of a young woman?

div.head: MAIL CARRIER
div.p: Coming in by herself, with a dog-puncher and an Indian?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Yes. Where did you pass her?

div.head: MAIL CARRIER
div.p: Yesterday afternoon, about three o'clock. They were making camp early. She was pretty tired from the looks of her.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: When should she get in?

div.head: MAIL CARRIER
div.p: I talked with the dog-puncher. He said they'd camp to-night at Mooseback and come in tomorrow. That's twenty-five miles, and if they don't start too late, they'll make Dawson by the middle of the day.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: What kind of a girl is she?

div.head: MAIL CARRIER
div.p: Good. How do you mean?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: I mean what kind of a looking girl is she? How did she strike you?

div.head: MAIL CARRIER
div.p: Oh, one of the soft and clingy kind, I guess I'd call her. You know, the kind that needs lots of cuddling and petting. Pretty, yes, danged pretty. Blue eyes, wavy hair, and all the rest—trembly lips and teary eyes—smily and weepy, you know, all in the same moment. But, gee! Freda, I can't stand here gassin' all day. I got about a thousand dollars' worth of letters to deliver—a dollar apiece and cheap at the price. I'll see you later. So long.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: All right, Joe. Tell Sitka Charley I want to see him, will you?

p.hi: (Mail Carrier returns to stove, picks up mail pouch, and sends Sitka Charley to Freda.)
(Capt. Eppingwell comes to Mail Carrier, and is leading him off to Mrs. Eppingwell when Dave Harney interposes.)

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: Hold your hosses, Joe. How about that dicker for the noospaper? You said Yes to fifty.

div.head: MAIL CARRIER

p.hi: (Pulling out his gold sack and drawing newspaper from pocket and giving both to Dave Harney.)

div.p: All right. Just weigh the fifty into that.

p.hi: (Dave Harney takes gold sack over to scales, produces his own gold sack, and a clerk weighs from one sack into the other.)
(Mail Carrier accompanies Capt. Eppingwell to Mrs. Eppingwell.)
(Capt. Eppingwell, Loraine Lisznayi, and Prince move along counter toward right and inspect mittens and moccasins.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: What time to-morrow has he decided upon starting?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: No to-morrow. To-day, to-night, twelve o'clock to-night.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: To-night! Are you sure?
Um.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: You said to-morrow.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Vanderlip um change mind. Look like much hurry.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: And the Lisznayi woman?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: She wait water-hole. Um meet her there. One Indian drive her dogs. Me drive Vanderlip's dogs.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: But Vanderlip mustn't go to-night.
Charley, he simply mustn't.
I tell you,

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Not only that, but you must help me to keep him from going.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: What for, Freda? I am Sitka Charley. I buy dogs, I sell dogs, I drive dogs. I help you dogs, yes. What for I help you other things? Vanderlip all the same one big chief. Um womans like um.
One, two, three womans like um. That um womans' trouble. No Sitka Charley's trouble. What for, Freda?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Why, what are you thinking about?
Sitka Charley I think you one big fool, Freda.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: And I think you are right, Charley, when I look back.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: No look back. Right now. What for you make fool with Vanderlip? Him no good. Him big fool too.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Oh, I see. You think I am in love with him.
Sitka Charley (With satisfaction.)
Um.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: You really think so?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um. What for you say he must no go to-night? Um?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Listen, Charley. You must help me, and I'll tell you all about it. There is a little girl coming in over the ice to marry Vanderlip—

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: One more woman! Um Vanderlip one dam big chief.
One woman, two woman, three woman, four womans.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: (Surprised.) Four women?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um. Four womans.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Who are they?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Little girl come in over ice—one. Lisznayi woman go 'way with um—two. Freda no want Lisznayi woman go 'way with um—three. Mrs. Eppingwell—four. One—two—three—four—womans.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Mrs. Eppingwell! Oh, you told me about her once. She was the woman who was with you on that trip through the Hills of Silence. She is a very brave woman. I have heard much of her, and I like her. If I were a man, I could love her. She must be very good, and sweet, and kind.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Sure. And um hard like iron sometimes. But um no like you. Um say so. What for um no like you?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: No woman likes me, Charley.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: All men like you.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: All men are fools.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: What for womans no like you?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: (Meditatively).
And she likes Vanderlip. How do you know? What do you know?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: No can tell. I promise.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Promised whom?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Mrs. Eppingwell. Um Mrs. Eppingwell very good woman.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: But she has a husband. It is not good for her to like another man. What do you think?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: I think I don't know. I think all um womans crazy. What for all um womans like this Vanderlip man?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Well, I don't.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Let me show you, Charley, and then you will know why I want you to help me. And, remember, you mustn't tell a word of any of this to any one.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um—maybe I tell Mrs. Eppingwell.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Don't be silly, Charley. You mustn't tell anybody. Promise me now.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: (With despairing perplexity.) All right, I no tell.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Now this little girl is coming in over the ice—her name is Flossie. She has lived a soft life down in California, where the sun is warm and there is no snow. She does not know hardship, nor the trail, and she is having a hard time now on the trail. Think of it!—sixty-five degrees below zero this morning, and she is out in it, walking, walking, walking, her breath freezing, her mouth icing up, her eyebrows rimed with frost. And she is very stiff, and sore, and tired. Every step of the trail she takes in pain. It is like a bad dream to her, Charley. But she sees, always before her, at the end of the dream, an awakening at Dawson, in the arms of the man who is to marry her. But, Charley, what if when she gets to Dawson there is no Floyd Vanderlip? no man to marry her? It will break her heart. It will be no happy awakening from a bad dream, but the beginning of a worse dream. And she is a little girl, Charley—not a strong woman like me who does not care. She will care, and she will know nobody, and she will cry, and cry, and cry. Did you ever hear a woman cry, Charley? Think of it, she is only a little girl.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um. More like baby.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Yes, put it that way, more like a baby. She cannot stand pain.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Oh, on trail, too much walk make um hurt.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: No, no.
Pain here.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um. I know. Um sick. What um call heart disease. I see one man sick that way. Um fall down dead, just like that.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Oh, you don't understand.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: I don't know. Womans all crazy.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: I think I can explain. Last summer you were in a canoe race on the river. You paddled very hard, but you lost.
And it hurt you—

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um. Um. Paddle like hell. No win race. (Stroking first one arm and then the other.) Much tired right here.
And um much hurt right here, no tired, just hurt like rheumatism, because I am sorry I lose race.
Um. Um.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: The very thing. She doesn't know it, but she is racing against this Lisznayi woman. Flossie must get here before the other woman steals her man. And you must help her win the race. Will you?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: You know this Flossie girl?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: No.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: No?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Never saw her in my life. But she is coming into a strange country without a friend or a dollar when she gets here. She will have great trouble. And you know, Charley, it is not good for a woman to be without friends or money in this country.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Don't know Flossie girl. No like Vanderlip man. What for you care?... Much foolishness. All womans crazy.... All right, I help.

p.hi: (Mail Carrier has-finished interview with Mrs. Eppingwell, received gold sack back from Dave Harney, and gone out with mail pouch to left. Capt. Eppingwell and Loraine Lisznayi have rejoined Mrs. Eppingwell.)
(Loraine Lisznayi says good-by to them, and starts to make exit to right, passing close to Freda and Sitka Charley. She pauses one or two paces away.)

div.head: LORAINE

p.hi: (Favoring Freda with a quick but sweeping, scornful glance.)

div.p: Come here, Charley. I want to speak to you a moment.

p.hi: (Her conduct angers Sitka Charley, who grows stolid and refuses to move or reply.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Speak with her, Charley.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: No speak.

p.hi: (Loraine Lisznayi, scornful expression on face, proceeds on her way, and makes exit to right.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Why didn't you, Charley?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: What for she look at you that way?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: They say she is a rich woman in her own country. But I don't believe it. I think she is after Vanderlip's money.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Lisznayi woman no got money. I know. I sell her dogs—eight hundred dollars. She pay me three hundred. Two weeks, three weeks, I no get other five hundred dollars. Um no got five hundred. I say, "My dogs, give me back." She give back. Me have fur robe. Good fur robe. She buy, two hundred dollar. Um no pay. Um have good fur robe. Me no have nothing. Um have cabin. Um no pay rent to Johnson. Um smile very nice, um Johnson wait. I know, I see. Um dogs she got now, Vanderlip give, make present. Um no pay firewood. Um no pay many things.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: I thought so. And now to win the race. Dogs first of all. Flossie must be brought in to-night. I want you here in Dawson, Charley. So you must send some Indian up the trail with a fresh team of dogs. Flossie camps at Mooseback tonight. He is to let her think that Vanderlip has sent the dogs, and that Vanderlip wants her to come right on to-night. Understand?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um. Sure.

div.head: FREDA

p.hi: (Preparing to start toward door at right.)

div.p: Start the dogs right away with a man you can trust. And he must be sure to let Flossie think that Vanderlip sent him. At the best, Flossie can't arrive until late to-night. And there may be delays. You keep on Vanderlip's trail so that you will know always where he is.

p.hi: (Freda and Sitka Charley start to walk toward the door at right.)

div.p: When I send for him you must bring him to me, and I'll hold him till Flossie gets in.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: No very strong, Freda.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Vanderlip no very strong, Charley.

p.hi: (Both cover ears, pull on mittens, and go out.)

(Dave Harney, unobserved, has been squatting on hams in front of counter to right, intently reading newspaper. He is making dumb show of excited interest. One of the miners discovers him, runs over to him, and starts to read newspaper over his shoulder. Dave Harney folds newspaper across, resting it on his knee, and looks up coolly into face of Miner.)

div.head: MINER
div.p: Can't you give a fellow a squint at your paper?

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: Got any sugar?
Sure.

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: Give me a whack at your sugar barrel?

div.head: MINER
div.p: No.

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: Then nary squint at my noospaper.

p.hi: (In meantime other miners and clerks have surrounded him, all demanding to see his newspaper. Whereupon he puts paper in his pocket, rises to his feet, and starts toward door to right, miners and clerks following him and grumbling at his meanness.)

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: You think you're smart, don't you? Got a corner on sugar, eh? And poor Dave Harney left without no sweetenin' for his coffee an' mush. Well, poor Dave Harney's got a corner on noos. When you want noos, come an' see him, an' be sure an bring your sugar along.

p.hi: (Mrs. Eppingwell and Capt. Eppingwell come forward to stove and warm their hands.)

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Perhaps Freda doesn't know about Flossie. I always thought her a good girl at heart.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Why this haste then? Why are they running away to-night instead of to-morrow as they had planned? They must have received information somehow, even before the mail carrier arrived. (Enter Mail Carrier from left.)
And look how she captured the mail carrier at once, and for one thing, I know, to learn Flossie's whereabouts.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Here he is now. Let's ask him.
You were talking with Freda a little while ago. What did she want to learn?

div.head: MAIL CARRIER
div.p: (Pausing only long enough to reply, and then going on to make exit to right.) Same thing as your wife—where I passed that girl's outfit.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: I knew it.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: But why couldn't I go around, or you, and talk with Freda, explain the situation fully to her, and make an appeal to whatever good is in her?
Mrs. Eppingwell (Smiling.)
You don't know women, Archie,
Well as women know women. No, she must be beaten at her own game. Flossie must arrive before midnight to-night.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: But she camps at Mooseback.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: There are dogs in Dawson. Now, Archie, this is for you to do. Borrow a team of fresh dogs somewhere, put your Indian in charge of it, that one-eyed man, he's faithful, and start him up the trail to Flossie. Let her think Floyd Vanderlip has sent the dogs to bring her in right away.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Ah, I see. The impatience of the ardent and long-denied lover.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: And once Flossie is here and gets her arms around Floyd Vanderlip's neck, Freda Moloof will wait in vain at the water-hole.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: That will settle it. Freda's not the woman to stand knocking her feet around a water-hole very long for any man.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: You seem to know a great deal about what kind of a woman this dancer is.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: I know enough about her, when it comes to Vanderlip and Flossie, to think her the best of the boiling... and to have a sneaking regret for her being beaten this way.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: You may be kind-hearted, Archie, but you are unwise.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Oh, well, after the manner of civilized man I submit to my womenkind. All right, I'll send the dogs at once.

p.hi: (Makes a movement to start toward door to right, and Mrs. Eppingwell starts with him.)
(Mrs. Eppingwell, struck suddenly by a new idea, pauses. Capt. Eppingwell pauses a step in advance and looks at her.)

div.p: What's wrong now?

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Suppose there is some mischance, a delay, and Flossie doesn't get in by midnight?

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Then Freda wins.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: No, she doesn't.

Floyd Vanderlip is coming to the ball. I'll see that he comes. I'll be very nice to him and watch him closely so that he does not sneak away. If Flossie fails to arrive, say by half-past eleven, I'll be taken ill, and I'll ask Vanderlip to take me home; and I'll hold him, no matter how terribly ill or terribly nice I have to be, until midnight is well past or until Flossie arrives.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Then it's my duty to disappear about the time you are taken ill.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Archie, though I tell you for the thousandth time, you are a perfect dear. And I can be as terribly nice as I please to Floyd Vanderlip?

p.hi: (Capt. Eppingwell laughs and nods, and they continue toward door.)

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL

p.hi: (While they are pulling on mittens, etc.)

div.p: And now the dogs. Don't delay a moment, Archie, please.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: The one-eyed man and the six dogs start at once.

p.hi: (Only clerks behind counter are left on the stage.)

(Nothing happens for a full minute, when Mrs. McFee appears at right, peeping through door, which she holds ajar. She peers cautiously about, enters, and sniffs the air several times. Then she smiles a sour smile of satisfaction.)

div.p: MRS. McFEE
And now a decent body can make her purchases.

div.head: ACT II—ANTEROOM OF PIONEER HALL
div.p: Scene. Anteroom of Pioneer Hall. It is ten-thirty P.M. The room is large and bare. Its walls are of logs, stuffed between with brown moss. Street door to rear, in centre. Doors, window-frames, and sashes of rough, unstained pine boards. At one side of door is wisp-broom for brushing snow from moccasins. On either side of door is an ordinary small-paned window, and beneath either window is a rough wooden bench. Under benches are large out-door moccasins, left there after the manner of overshoes, by their owners. In available space on rear wall, many wooden pegs, on which are hanging furs, parkas, hats, wraps, etc. Midway between front and rear, and at equal distances between centre and sides, running at full blast, are two large wood-burning stoves. Alongside each stove is a wood-box filled with firewood. On right, a window. On left, wide doorway, open, connecting with ballroom. Through doorway come occasional snatches of dance-music, bursts of laughter and of voices. Because it is very cold, street door is kept closed, and is opened by doorkeeper only when some one knocks, and then only long enough for that one to enter. All parleying is done on inside with door closed. Prince, as doorkeeper, is standing at rear by street door. Men and women, in costume, are disappearing through door to left, from where come strains of a waltz.

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: (Drawing up his shoulders, as if cold.) B-r-r!
(Crosses rapidly to lejt and peers through doorway into ballroom, looking jor somebody. Holds up his finger and beckons.) Here, you, Billy! More fire! Hi yu skookum fire!

p.hi: (Enter Indian, who proceeds to fire up both stoves.)
(Prince stands looking into ballroom. A knock is heard at street door. He returns and opens door.)
(A Man enters, masked and in heavy fur overcoat.)

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: Hello.

p.hi: (The Man hesitates, looks around, and starts to cross to left.)

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: Well?

div.head: MAN

p.hi: (Pausing, and then, as if discovering reason for his detention.)

div.p: Oh!

p.hi: (Sits down on bench and proceeds to remove moccasins.)

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: Masks must be lifted at the door, you know.

div.head: MAN
div.p: And give myself away? Oh, no.

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: The doorkeeper's lips are sealed. I give nobody's identity away. Come on, let's see who you are.
Jack Denison!

div.head: MAN
div.p: Yours truly, Prince, my boy.

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: But you can't come in here, old man.

div.head: MAN
div.p: And why not?

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: Why—I—they're damned select—it's the women, you know—and I—they—well, they made me doorkeeper, and—
—you know well enough yourself, Jack.

div.head: MAN
div.p: (Rising as though to go, and in angry tones.) By God, you can come down to Jack Denison's joint all right, and buck Jack Denison's faro layout all right, and have a social drink with him all right; but when Jack Denison comes up to your doings, you turn'm down like he had smallpox.

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: It's not my fault. It's the women, I tell you. They're running the show.

div.head: MAN
div.p: You might let a fellow in just for a peep. Nobody'll know. I'll clear out before they unmask.

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: I can't really, old man, I—

p.hi: (Catches sight oj Mrs. McFee, who appears in doorway to left.)

div.p: Look at her! Get out quick!

p.hi: (Places hand on his shoulder in friendly way and starts to shove him out.)

div.head: MAN
div.p: Wow!

p.hi: (With bodily expression of fear, shrinks behind Prince and allows himself to be shoved out.)

div.p: MRS. McFEE
(Crossing over to Prince, and suspiciously.) Who might that body be?

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: One of the unelect, I am sorry to say, Mrs. McFee.
MRS. McFEE
A gambler man, I take it?
But I can no see, Mr. Prince, why you should conduct negotiations inside the door, contameenating the air with the bodily presence of the children of sin.

div.head: PRINCE

p.hi: (Slight note of anger in his voice.)

div.p: Do you know how cold it is, Mrs. McFee?

div.head: MRS. MCFEE
div.p: I have no given it a thought.

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: Well, it's seventy degrees below zero, and still going down. If that door is open one minute, a refrigerator would be comfortable alongside that ballroom. And if you don't like the way I'm doing things—

p.hi: (A knock is heard, and he opens door. Sitka Charley squeezes in.)

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: Can Sitka Charley come in, Mrs. McFee?
MRS. McFEE
He is a good body. There is no reason why he should not bide a wee.
But you must go right away again, Charley.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: (Nods his head, and then to Prince.) Where um Vanderlip?

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: He's here somewhere. Go and find him.

p.hi: (Laughter and voices, and many couples enter from lejt, some in costume, several in hooded dominos.)

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: What that?
What for? Everybody crazy?

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: Button, button, who's got the button. Go and find him.

p.hi: (Sitka Charley, walking stealthily, like a wild animal in dangerous territory, goes adventuring amongst the maskers.)
(After some time, a domino takes Sitka Charley by the arm and leads him apart.)

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: (Dragging back and struggling to escape.) What for, crazymans?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Shut up! It's me, Vanderlip. Looking for me?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Anything wrong?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: No wrong. All right. Um Freda want you come right away.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Freda! What's she want with me?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um no tell. Um say: "Charley, you go Pioneer Hall quick. All the same one big dance. You catch um Vanderlip. You make um come right away."

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Where?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um Freda's cabin. You come now?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: (Thinks for a minute, with a bothered air.) I'll come in a little while. You tell her.

p.hi: (Turns to rejoin dancers, and speaks over shoulder.)

div.p: Dogs all right?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Be at the water-hole at twelve o'clock?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um. Sure.

p.hi: (Sitka Charley gains street door and goes out.)

(A knock is heard at door. Enter Dave Harney, costumed as a Scotch minister. He passes Prince's inspection, removes street moccasins and parka, and walks to the front. His shambling, loose-jointed gait discovers him. There is hand-clapping and laughter, and there are cries of "Harney! Harney!" "Dave Harney!" Crowd singsy "For the sugar-man will catch you if you don't watch out." He accepts the discovery, goes over to stove at right, pulls newspaper out of pocket, and begins to read. The dancers crowd about him, demanding the news. He makes to be offended by them and walks away, reading paper. They follow behind him, still clamoring for the news. He promenades about stage and then makes exit to left, followed by the whole crew, with the exception of one domino and a Court Lady of the time of Louis XVI, who linger by stove to left.)

div.head: COURT LADY
div.p: Mrs. Eppingwell I haven't seen your make-up, Archie.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Domino,
Would that I might claim Archie for myself, there is such affectionate possession in the way you say it. Who is this Archie, sweet lady?

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Come, come, Archie, a truce to fooling. Besides, you can't fool me anyway. Did you get the dogs off?

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Promptly, and with the one-eyed man. Also a spare man to come back post-haste and let us know their progress.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Then when should Flossie arrive?

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: We figured it out. Barring accidents, or the unusual, she'll be here by eleven-thirty—at any rate, not later than midnight.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Not later than midnight.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Of course, after all, one can't tell within an hour.
Mrs. Eppingwell And she is to be brought here?

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: She'll ride the sled right up to the door. A knock, and then, enter Flossie.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: And then all our troubles will be over. And now for your make-up. I insist.

p.hi: (Capt. Eppingwell slips off domino and stands forth a faithful copy of Sitka Charley.)

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Sitka Charley!

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Um wantum dogs? I sell um dogs, much good dogs.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Excellent!

p.hi: (She catches sight of Sitka Charley, who is entering through street door at rear.)

div.p: Quick!
Now let us return to the ballroom and find Floyd Vanderlip. I'm pretty sure of him. He's in a domino, too.

p.hi: (They start for exit to left. Sitka Charley, mistaking Capt. Eppingwell for Vanderlip, signals to him a desire to speak with him, but is ignored. Exit Mrs. Eppingwell and Capt. Eppingwell. Sitka Charley stands a moment, puzzled, watching them go, then follows after them. Makes, exit, and a moment later enters with Vanderlip, who is still in domino.)

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: What do you want now?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Me no want. Freda want.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: What's she want?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Want you.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: I haven't anything to do with her. She can keep on wanting. I'm busy.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um want you now, right away, quick.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: You go to the devil. And she can go, too, for all I care.

p.hi: (Enter Dave Harney from left, still reading newspaper, and followed by the dancers.)

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: I tell Freda you say go to devil?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Tell her! Tell her! Just as long as you quit bothering me.
And when you've told her you'd better go and see everything's in shape.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Dogs, sleds, everything all right.

div.head: DAVE HARNEY

p.hi: (In centre of stage, turning suddenly upon rout at his heels.)

div.p: Well? What d'ye want?

p.hi: (The rout gathers about him, facing him. There are cries of: "The news! The news!" "What's happening down in God's country?" "Who won the championship?" "How'd the election turn out?" "Was Tammany downed?" "Is it true the United States is fighting Germany?" "Is war really declared?" etc.)

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: Got any sugar?
A Voice
The meanest man in the Klondike.

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: So you'd be, dodgast you, if you hadn't no sweetenin' for your coffee and mush.
Another Voice Speech! Speech!
Voices
Speech! Speech!

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: All right, consarn you, I'll speechify.
Ladies an' gentlemen—ahem—

div.head: A VOICE
div.p: Bring him some water. A glass of water, please, for the speaker.

div.head: ANOTHER VOICE
div.p: Get a box for him.

p.hi: (The firewood is dumped out of the wood-box, which is placed before Dave Harney upside down. He is helped upon it.)

div.head: A VOICE
div.p: Now he's going to read us all the news. (Cheers and hand-clapping.)

div.head: DAVE HARNEY

p.hi: (Folding newspaper and putting it in his pocket.)

div.p: My friend, you've got another guess comin'. I'm goin' to read you the riot act. An' here it is, short an' simple. You've got all the sugar, an' I've got all the noos. Nothin' to it but a dicker. We'll swop. That's what we'll do, we'll swop. (Cheers.)
An' I say again, for them as is dull of hearin', we'll swop. After the unmaskin', you all will assemble here in this here room an' hear the noospaper read, advertisements an' all.

An' in the meantime, I'm open to subscriptions in the form of promissory notes. Said notes shall be for the sum of one heapin', large tin cup of sugar, white or brown, to be paid to party of the first part—you all is party to the second part—to be paid to party of the first part inside twenty-four hours after the delivery of the goods, to wit, the noos. Said party of the first part hereby agreein' to send a man with a sack around to the cabins of said party of the second part an' collect face value of promissory note, to wit, one heapin', large tin cup of sugar, white or brown. Them that signs notes hears the noospaper read, them that don't, don't. Thankin' you kindly, one an' all, I remain, yours truly, an' am ready to take promissory notes here an' now.

div.head: A VOICE
div.p: But we haven't any pen or ink, Dave.

div.head: DAVE HARNEY
div.p: You've got to sit up all night to get up earlier than Dave Harney in the mornin'. Here you are.

p.hi: (Draws pen, inkstand, and paper pad from pockets.)

div.p: An' you might as well sign first, young feller.

p.hi: (The signing of notes begins, Dave Harney, with ink and paper, passing from one to another as the rout breaks up and starts back to ballroom for next dance.)

div.p: Just as easy—like shooting fish in a bucket.

p.hi: (Enter Mrs. Eppingwell on arm of Vanderlip, who is still in domino. They promenade, talking, about room. They are followed by Loraine Lisznayi, masked and magnificently costumed, who keeps her eyes on them and betrays keen interest in them.)

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Wasn't it funny I guessed you, Mr. Vanderlip, in that first dance?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: You have a good eye.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: And possibly I really wanted to find you, you know.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Hum, yes, I suppose so. And I was looking for you, too, hard as I could.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: You'd never guess how I guessed you.
It is very simple. You are the same height as Captain Eppingwell.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Hello, I haven't the next dance with you!

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: No, that's promised to—well, to somebody else.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: But the next after is mine.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: And the next after that. I'm almost afraid I'm dancing too much with you. What will people say?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Ah, but they don't know who we are.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: They will after the unmasking. Then they will remember us together so much.

div.head: VANDERLIP

p.hi: (As though struck by a thought of something else.)

div.p: What time will they unmask?

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Two o'clock. And (Looks at card.) there is a waltz after that I should like. You do waltz so well, Mr. Vanderlip.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: I won't be able to make that waltz, I—(Breaks off suddenly.)

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Why, you, of all men, are not going home early?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: No—I—that is—

p.hi: (Looks at card, studies it profoundly, as though it would get him out of his difficulty.)

div.p: Why, yes, of course we can have that waltz together. I thought it was already engaged, that was all.

p.hi: (Enter Capt. Eppingwell, who comes up to them, still in domino.)

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: The next is mine, I believe, fair lady.

p.hi: (Vanderlip ranges up alongside of him and measures height of shoulders. Capt. Eppingwell curiously observes the action, and speaks with gruff voice.)

div.p: Well, stranger, what's up?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: We're both up.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Up to what?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Up to each other. We're the same height, and I've guessed you, Captain Eppingwell.

p.hi: (All laugh together, and Capt. Eppingwell bears Mrs. Eppingwell away. They make exit to left.)

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: A word in your ear, sir.
All is discovered.
Your actions have betrayed you.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Who are you?

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: Never mind who I am. I know.
(Takes his hand and looks at palm.) You are about to make a long journey.
I see a water-hole.
I hear a clock strike twelve.
She is a dark woman, a foreigner.
And her name is—
(In natural voice, laughing.) Loraine.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: You fooled me all right, Loraine. You said you weren't coming to the ball.

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: I didn't intend to, but everything was packed and ready for the start, and I had nothing to do. So I came.
Floyd, don't you think you've been dancing with that Mrs. Eppingwell rather frequently?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: No, I don't.

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: You've danced every dance with her.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Somebody else is dancing with her now.

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: And, in consequence, you are not dancing at all.

div.head: VANDERLIP

p.hi: (Making movement to take her into ballroom.)

div.p: Come, then, let us dance it together.

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: No.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Aw, come on.

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: No.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: All right, then, don't.

div.head: LORAINE

p.hi: (After a pause, softly, hesitatingly, tears in voice, etc.)

div.p: Floyd—I—

p.hi: (Breaks down and weeps in feminine way.)
(Vanderlip is soft as mush at once. His arm is around her, and she is drawn close to him.)

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: There, there, dear. You know I love you.

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: I—I am jealous, Floyd. I know it, but I can't help it. You are a man to touch women's hearts. They can't help loving you, and—and—

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Oh, pshaw. Anyway, you are the one woman, or I wouldn't be taking you down river to-night.

p.hi: (Prince has gone to left and is looking into ballroom, so they are unobserved.)

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: Yes, yes, I know. Forgive me. And now I must be going.
(They move to rear to street door. He helps her on with moccasins and street wraps.) Aren't you coming, too?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: No, not yet. But I'll be on time.

p.hi: (She glances at Prince's back, lifts mask, and raises face for kiss. He bends and kisses her.)

div.head: LORAINE
div.p: At the water-hole.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: At twelve sharp.

p.hi: (She kisses him again, clings to him, and goes out.)
(At sound of door shutting, Prince turns around, then returns to street door.)

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: Hello!

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Hello. How d'ye like the job?

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: I wouldn't undertake it again for all the gold in Klondike.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Losing all your friends, eh?

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: Half of them. They, will butt in, and I have to turn them away. Oh, it's hospitality, you bet. I've been with them on trail, I've eaten their food and slept in their blankets, and now I turn them away from the merrymaking of myself and my friends.
There's one, now.
No, it's only Sitka Charley.

p.hi: (Enter Sitka Charley, who draws Vanderlip to one side.)

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: You come?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: No, I tell you. No.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: No come?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Then um Freda come. She say, you no come, she come. Sure.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Come here?

p.hi: (He shakes his head and laughs incredulously.)

div.p: Not on your life.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: No come?

p.hi: (Vanderlip goes to rear, takes off domino, disclosing himself as a cowboy. Hangs domino on wall. Takes down from wall a sombrero, which he puts on head. Makes exit to left.)
(Prince, who is now alone, walks over to stove at left, adjusts damper, and warms his hands.)
(The street door is cautiously opened, without knocking, and Sitka Charley puts head inside and peers around. Withdraws head.)

(Street door is again cautiously opened, this time the masked face of a woman appearing, and then Freda, in long cloak, enters. She removes street moccasins, revealing dancing slippers on her feet, and puts moccasins under bench close to door. She removes cloak, and reveals herself in a striking evening gown. As she turns her back to hang cloak on wall, Prince happens to see her. She starts toward ballroom, but he steps in her way and stops her.)

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: I beg your pardon.
I am the doorkeeper, you know.
The instructions are that all masks must be lifted at the door.

p.hi: (Still silence On part of Freda. The situation is awkward for Prince, and he begins again.)

div.p: I don't know who you are, but the rules are imperative. I must see your face.

p.hi: (Steps forward and lifts his hand to raise mask.)

div.head: FREDA

p.hi: (Quickly stepping back and speaking in a slightly muffled voice.)

div.p: You will be sorry if you see my face.

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: I have been made sorry by more than one face I've seen to-night and turned away from the door.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: But in my case you will be sorry for quite a different reason.

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: For what reason, then, pray?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Because, after seeing my face, you will not turn me away.

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: Then there will be no reason for me to turn you away.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: On the contrary, all the reason in the world. But you won't.

p.hi: (Prince laughs incredulously. Mrs. Mc-Fee appears in doorway to left, looks suspiciously at them, and disappears.)

div.p: So it will be better, Stanley, if you let me in without seeing my face.

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: (Starting at her use of his given name.) You know me!—er—well!

div.head: FREDA
div.p: And you know me well. Now let me pass. Some day I will tell you about it, my reason for coming here, and you will be glad.

p.hi: (She starts as though to go to the ballroom.)

div.head: PRINCE

p.hi: (Springing in her way and seizing her arm.)

div.p: No you don't, my lady! Enough fooling. Let me see your face.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: There have been times when you treated me less roughly. For the sake of those times, let me pass.

div.head: PRINCE
