p.hi: (Still retaining hold on her arm, and after hesitating for a moment.)

div.p: No, it's a bluff you're running on me. I don't know who you are, but I'm going to find out.

p.hi: (He lifts free hand toward her mask.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: You will be sorry.
Be in ignorance of me, and let me pass. It will be better so.

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: If you have no right, I'll not let you pass anyway. Now let me see you.

p.hi: (Still holding her by one arm, he tries to lift mask.)
(Mrs. McFee appears in doorway to left and watches suspiciously.)
(Sitka Charley knocks and then enters through street door, Prince giving a quick glance in his direction and ascertaining that it is all right for him to enter.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Stanley!

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: (Releasing her and speaking with awe.) No! Not you!

p.hi: (Freda lifts her mask, her back to Mrs. McFee, and for several seconds, her face serious with resolve, her eyes flashing, she gazes upon him. She lowers mask, and makes as though to start toward door to left. He hesitates, stands aside, then hesitates again.)

div.p: It is all my social standing in Dawson is worth, to—to let you pass.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: I told you you would be sorry.
There is Sitka Charley. I want to speak to him. And there's that psalm-singer in the doorway. Don't let her suspect me.

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: I shall resign my post.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Resign? You will be of more help to me if you retain it.

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: I have been unfaithful to it. Pass, Freda, pass. Who am I to say you nay?

p.hi: (He leaves her and returns to street door. Freda goes over to Sitka Charley. Mrs. McFee disappears jrom doorway, but reappears one or two times to stare suspiciously.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: How is Vanderlip dressed? What does he look like?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um all the same long black dress, like um woman.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Dressed as a woman!

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: No dress woman. Um like—um—um—like um priest man.

p.hi: (Makes motion of hand around head to describe hood of domino, and motion down to his feet to describe length of domino.)

div.p: Um long black, like priest man.

p.hi: (A domino, with lady on arm, appears in doorway, as though about to enter, then changing mind, disappears.)

div.p: Look see! Just like that. That um Vanderlip.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: All right, Charley. I understand. And now for you. Flossie can't get here too quickly. You must take dogs, fresh dogs, up the trail, and when you meet her, put her on your sled, and race in with her as fast as you can. Tell her Vanderlip sent you and is waiting for her.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um dogs, fresh dogs, have not got.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Take my dogs. You know them.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um best dogs in Klondike. Sure.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: And bring Flossie straight to my cabin. Don't stop anywhere else for anything. Right up to the door and in with her. Understand?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um Vanderlip there?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Yes, Vanderlip will be there waiting for her.
Now hurry.

p.hi: (To Prince, who is standing forlornly at his post.)

div.p: I'm sorry, Stanley, but I had to do this thing. Now I want to find Floyd Vanderlip.

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: You'll find him in the ballroom. Black domino—you know his height.

div.head: FREDA

p.hi: (Resting one hand on his arm and laughing cheerily.)

div.p: There, there, don't look so glum. All is not lost. Nobody will know me, and I'll be gone in five minutes.

p.hi: (Mrs. McFee appears in doorway to left. Looks at them standing together.)
(Freda crosses to left and goes out, Mrs. McFee standing aside and looking at her closely.)

div.p: MRS. McFEE
Who might that woman be, Mr. Prince?

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: The doorkeeper's lips are sealed. Those were my instructions. The doorkeeper can disclose identities to nobody.
MRS. McFEE
But to me—

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: To nobody. You are made no exception, Mrs. McFee. And furthermore, I'm going to resign.
MRS. McFEE
Resign!

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: And right now. And whoever takes my place—you'd better put a mask on him, or he'll lose all his friends as I have.

div.head: MRS. MCFEE
div.p: Your friends, the kind of men and women you turned from this door?

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: Yes, my friends, men and women, children of sin, lost, hopeless wretches,—my friends.
MRS. McFEE

p.hi: (Sniffing and tossing her head, and very frigidly.)

div.p: I believe it is just as well, Mr. Prince. I had my doots of you all along. There is no telling what base creatures you have admitted. I shall get an honorable man to guard the door. I shall inform the committee—

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: Get him! Get him! Go get him! You can't be any too quick for me!

div.head: MRS. MCFEE
div.p: You are a shame and a disgrace, and when I bring your conduct before the committee—

div.head: PRINCE
div.p: If you don't go right away and get some one to take my place, I'll throw open the door and call in the scum of the town.
MRS. McFEE
No! No! Dinna be rash!

p.hi: (Several couples have entered from ballroom and are promenading, among them Capt. Eppingwell, by himself, in domino.)
(Enter Sitka Charley through street door, looking for some one. He mistakes Capt. Eppingwell for Vanderlip.)

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Hello, Vanderlip. You no come Freda's cabin you catch um hell, sure.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Hello. What's Freda want with me.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY

p.hi: (Recognizing that it is not Vanderlip's voice, and surprised.)

div.p: You no Vanderlip?

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: No. Me Sitka Charley.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: What for, crazymans? Me Sitka Charley.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Me Sitka Charley.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: No, me.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: No, me.

p.hi: (He suddenly takes off domino, disclosing himself in make-up of Sitka Charley. Sitka Charley gazes at him dumbfounded. Rubs his eyes.)

div.p: You buy um dogs, good dogs, I sell.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: You me. Who me?
What for? Everybody crazy. Me crazy too.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL

p.hi: (Struck by an idea, he puts on domino again, and drags Sitka Charley by arm to back of room.)

div.p: Come on, we'll have some fun.

p.hi: (Feels in pocket of overcoat hanging on wall and brings out a mask, which he puts on Sitka Charley.)

div.p: Now for fun!

p.hi: (Capt. Eppingwell takes Sitka Charley to left, thrusts him into ballroom, and remains in doorway, watching.)
(Enter Freda. Capt. Eppingwell stands aside for her to pass. But she stops and measures his height and build with her eye.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: At last I've found you, Floyd.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: I like that, guessing me the first time. And who are you?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Oh! It was a mistake.

p.hi: (Starts to leave him, but he follows her, detaining her.)

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Not so fast, fair lady. I've an idea you'll dance—
—the next quadrille, let us say.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: I think it's engaged. I've lost my programme.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL

p.hi: (Putting hand inside domino and bringing forth a programme.)

div.p: I have a spare one. Allow me.

p.hi: (Enter Sitka Charley from left, running away from Clown, who is striking him on back with bladder.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Thank you. The next quadrille then. (Looking at Sitka Charley.)
There is somebody I wish to speak to. Good-by.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Good-by.

p.hi: (Mrs. McFee enters from left with man, whom she takes to street door and who relieves Prince, who makes exit to left.)
(Freda joins in pursuit of Sitka Charley and drives Clown away.)
(Mrs. McFee watches Freda and Sitka Charley.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: I thought you had started up the trail with the dogs long ago. Anything the matter?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Me come back speak to you. Me think, um Lisznayi woman wait at water-hole, no Vanderlip come, maybe she make much trouble. Much better Lisznayi woman go long way off. Maybe I think very good tell Lisznayi woman lie. Maybe say Vanderlip meet her twenty mile down trail. One Indian man take her on sled twenty mile down trail, then she sure make no trouble.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: A good idea. You hurry and fix it up, quick, and then start after Flossie.

One moment, Charley. Ten miles down river is Salmon Stake. One missionary man lives at Salmon Stake. Tell Indian man to take Lisznayi woman to missionary house and knock on door. Missionary man gets out of bed and lets them in. Indian man tells missionary man that Lisznayi woman come to see him, come to be good woman.
Understand?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Very good. Dam good. All right.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: And hurry as fast as you can.

p.hi: (Freda, looking over one after another of couples and groups, and watched suspiciously by Mrs. McFee, continues search for Vanderlip and goes to left.)
(Sitka Charley starts toward street door, but is interrupted by Mrs. McFee.)

div.head: MRS. MCFEE
div.p: Who is that woman?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Um crazy womans maybe.
MRS. McFEE
But who is she?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY

p.hi: (Stirring the air with his hand to describe general mix-up.)

div.p: Everybody somebody; somebody nobody; nobody anybody. What for? Sitka Charley no Sitka Charley. Sitka Charley somebody else. Somebody else Sitka Charley.
MRS. McFEE
You do it very well. Allow me to congratulate you.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: What for long words? Sitka Charley don't know long words.
MRS. McFEE
Oh, I know you, Captain Eppingwell.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Me no Captain Eppingwell. Me Sitka Charley.

div.head: MRS. MCFEE
div.p: You do it excellently. Even I would be almost deceived, I assure you, Captain Eppingwell.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Me Captain Eppingwell?
MRS. McFEE
Of course you are. I knew you at once.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Mrs. Eppingwell my squaw?

div.head: MRS. MCFEE
div.p: Yes, and Mrs. Eppingwell is your wife. Now tell me who that woman was.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Me no drink whiskey all day. Yet me all the same drunk. Me no me. Me Captain Eppingwell. Me have one fine squaw. Wow! (Soberly, holding one hand to head and shaking head.)
Sitka Charley much sick. Sitka Charley go home. (Starts for street door, but Mrs. McFee detains him.)
MRS. McFEE
No, no, Captain, you are coming with me to see how the supper is being laid, and you are going to tell me who that woman is.

p.hi: (Sitka Charley does not want to go, but, vainly protesting, is lugged off by Mrs. McFee through door to left.)

(Capt. Eppingwell, who has lingered about, watches them got and when gone he takes off domino, hangs same on wall, and discloses himself in make-up of Sitka Charley. He proceeds to put wood in stove to right.)
(Freda enters from left and sees Capt. Eppingwell bending over woodbox. She crosses over to him in an angry, determined way.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Still here! When I asked you to hurry!
Shame on you, Charley. Now go, as fast as you can.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: What for go? You buy dogs? I sell dogs, good dogs.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Oh! You again!

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Me Sitka Charley.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: You are the man in the domino. I might have known you were not Sitka Charley. You are taller.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: And in the domino you mistook me because of my height.
Oh, I know. The man you seek is about my height, eh?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Who are you?

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Who are you?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: You don't know me. I am a new arrival in Dawson. I came in over the ice.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Now I have you! I met you to-day.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: No, you didn't.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Yes, I did. You are the Lisznayi—I beg pardon—Miss—er—Miss Lisznayi.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: It's a shame to be found out so quickly. Mister—? Mister—?

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Mr. Sitka Charley.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Well, then, Mr. Sitka Charley, I am displeased with you. You are too cunning. I am really vexed, and for punishment I am going to leave you.

p.hi: (She curtsies deeply, and walks away toward left.)

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: That voice. That walk! That carriage!
Fooled! Fooled! That's not the Lisznayi!

p.hi: (A voice, off stage, is heard calling, "Take partners for a quadrille!")

div.p: I beg pardon, but this dance is ours.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Yes, it is, but really, I must beg off. I—I don't like quadrilles.
There's a waltz two dances down. I'll give you that.

p.hi: (A man, in costume, appears in doorway to left, and shouts: "One more couple needed! Here, you! One more couple!")

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: There! We're needed.

p.hi: (Man in doorway, who has turned around and surveyed ballroom, turns back and calls: "Too late! Sets are full!" Opening bars of dance are heard.)

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL

p.hi: (Seizing Freda in his arms and starting to waltz.)

div.p: We'll make a waltz of it here.

p.hi: (They waltz a jew steps, Freda abandoning herself to it, when she suddenly stops and withdraws herselj from his arms.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Please let me go. You may have that waltz later.

p.hi: (She looks at watch and betrays her need for haste.)

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: There is something familiar about you. I have seen you before. I have danced with you before. And—well, I have never danced with the Lisznayi.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: No, you don't know me.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Let me tell you the occasion.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: There has been no occasion.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Nevertheless, let me tell you. It may interest you.
Here was the stove, here the piano. Three-fingered Jack played the fiddle. It was Old Dan Tucker that we danced. Remember?

There was the doorway to the front, always open. Through it came the clatter of chips, the rattle of roulette balls, the calls of the gamekeepers. And there was the rear door. It opened upon the street. When it opened the frost came through, in a cloud of vapor, rolling along the floor and hiding the feet and legs of the dancers to the knees. And we danced, you and I, we danced Old Dan Tucker.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: How interesting! Tell me, that—that what you described, it is a—a dance-hall? Am I right?

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: I remember when you came in through the door. The frost rolled in with you, and you wore the most magnificent furs in all the Klondike. And you danced in moccasins, in little red moccasins. Remember?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Ah, those furs! Is there a woman in the land who has not heard of them and envied their possessor, this woman you take me for—and I know who you mean—this—this dance-hall artist, this—this Freda Moloof. And how often have you danced with her?—with me, I mean.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Once. That one night. But I have seen her several times. Who has not?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Her? Me, you mean.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Yes, and one other thing. That accent!
Freda, it is you!

div.head: FREDA
div.p: At last I am discovered. Confess, sir, it took you some time.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: I do confess you puzzled me not a little. But what are you doing here? It's daring, to say the least.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Oh, I was weary for a change. I was yawning my head off. So I thought I'd come up and see if you and your select friends danced Old Dan Tucker as well as we danced it that—that night.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: But if you are discovered?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Only you could discover me.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: There is trouble brewing, Freda. Frankly, I believe it would be better for you to go.

p.hi: (Freda laughs long, a mocking, silvery laughter which perplexes and bewilders him.)

div.p: Come, come. What's the matter?
What's struck you so funny?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: (Quieting down, but holding hand to side.) It is better than I dreamed.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: What is better?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: My make-up.
Capt. Eppingwell (In doubt.)
Make-up?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: The make-up under my make-up, if you please.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL

p.hi: (With a faint glimmer of conviction this time.)

div.p: But the accent! You can't get away from it.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Far be it from me to get away from it. On the contrary, I sought after it, and I flatter myself that I got it pretty close to the original. I'd like to meet this Freda. I'll wager my accent is nearer hers than her own is.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Then who the deuce are you? Where could you have learned that accent?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Why, I was caught in a storm over on Indian River. We were compelled to seek shelter in a little cabin, and whom should we find there, likewise driven in by the storm, but this Freda Moloof. There was no standing on ceremony nor conventionality. It was life or death, and in I went. We were storm-bound two days. And she was very kind to me.

p.hi: (A pause, then, voice tender and sympathetic.)

div.p: I felt so sorry for her.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Well?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Well, I studied her, that is all.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Now I have you! You are the woman reporter of the Kansas City Star!

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Think so? Think so?
Now I am really going to leave you. I must. But don't forget that waltz.

p.hi: (She walks away and makes exit to left.)

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL

p.hi: (In utter bewilderment, watching her till she disappears.)

div.p: Well, I'll be damned.

p.hi: (He puts on domino and follows after her, still intent on discovering her identity, and makes exit to left.)
(The quadrille is over, and as he passes out, couples begin to enter from left.)
(Mrs. McFee and Sitka Charley enter from left. She still holds him captive, hanging on his arm.)

div.p: MRS. McFEE
(Ingratiatingly, making as near a simper as her sour mouth and age will permit.) You might have asked me to dance, Captain.

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Me no dance. Me much sick. Me crazy. Me drunk. Me go home.

p.hi: (Strives to get to street door, but she clings to his arm and holds him back.)

div.p: MRS. McFEE
Dinna you think by now, Captain, that you've convinced me what a fine actor you are?

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY

p.hi: (Striving for street door, but being held back, in final break-down of patience.)

div.p: What for, dam fool woman you?
MRS. McFEE
Oh!

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Crazy! Fool! Dam! What for?
MRS. McFEE
Oh! Oh! And I thought you were a gentleman! You have insulted me!

div.head: SITKA CHARLEY
div.p: Sure! Me insult. Much insult. Dam! Dam! Dam!
MRS. McFEE
Oh! This cannot be Captain Eppingwell. 'Tis some base creature from the town. I am contameenated!

p.hi: (Sticks fingers in ears and screams shrilly.)
(Many come running jrom ballroom at sound of screams. Sitka Charley still rages, shouting, "Dam! Dam! Dam!")
(Capt. Eppingwell comes in with some lady on arm and joins an onlooking group near stove to right. He still wears domino.)

div.p: MRS. McFEE
This vile creature has insulted me. Where is the doorkeeper?
Come you, Mr. McFarline, and eject this beast.

p.hi: (Doorkeeper starts forward. Clown startles Sitka Charley by unexpectedly hitting him a resounding blow with bladder between the shoulders. Sitka Charley runs in and out amongst people, pursued by Doorkeeper and Clown. The Doorkeeper is slow and ponderous, and falls down. At the moment he falls, Sitka Charley dashes into group where stands Capt. Eppingwell, whom he strips, with one rush, of domino. Sitka Charley swiftly puts domino on himself and dashes, on, still pursued by Clown, who is striking him with bladder. Both make exit to left.)

(Doorkeeper, getting up, mistakes Capt. Eppingwell for Sitka Charley, and proceeds to eject him. Capt. Eppingwell resists. Mrs. McFee urges on the Doorkeeper. In struggle, Capt. Eppingwell's mask comes off. Doorkeeper, in amazement, lets go of him. Capt. Eppingwell is angry, Mrs. McFee dumfounded, everybody excited.—Tableau.)

(Sitka Charley dashes in from left, pursued by Clown. Sitka Charley races madly across stage, like a dog with a tin can to its tail, and jerks open street door. Doorkeeper tries to stop him, clutches domino, but Sitka Charley plunges through and slams door after him, leaving domino in hands of Doorkeeper, who is nonplussed for a moment, then walks over and presents it to Capt. Eppingwell.)
(Excitement quiets down. Groups break up and begin to pass off stage to left.)
(Capt. Eppingwell, having lingered in order to recover his breath, goes to left rear and hangs up domino on wall.)
(Vanderlip, in costume of cowboy, and Mrs. Eppingwell are standing talking by stove to right front.)
(Freda enters alone from left and looks about. Recognizes Capt. Eppingwell and goes up to him.)

div.p: Capt. Eppingwell (Gallantly.)
Ah, mysterious fair one!

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Surely you have guessed me by now.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: I was never so befooled in my life. I could swear I know you, but to save me I can't put my finger on you.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: You may if you wish.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: What?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: I say you may know me if you wish.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: How?—When?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Now.

p.hi: (He eagerly makes to lift mask and learn her identity. She steps hand quickly, with one hand holding him off.)

div.p: No, no; there are certain stipulations.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL

p.hi: (Displaying in advance a willingness to consent.)

div.p: Yes, yes.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: First, you must ask no questions.
Second, you must tell nobody.
And third, you must point out to me Floyd Vanderlip.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: I agree. Now who are you?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: But you haven't pointed out Floyd Vanderlip.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: There he is.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: And with whom is he talking?

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL

p.hi: (Starting as though to answer, then changing his mind.)

div.p: That was not in the bond. Now who are you?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Guess.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: I call that cruel. I've exhausted my guesses. (Freda lifts mask and gazes at him for several seconds, her face serious, her eyes flashing.)

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: (Giving a long whistle of comprehension.) Freda!

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Even so, Freda. And I thank you. And I shall have yet more to thank you for. That waltz—you must let me off.
Capt. Eppingwell There is no reason. Let me have it.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Impossible. I shall be gone.
Why, it is half-past eleven! I am going now, in a minute.
Capt. Eppingwell With Vanderlip?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: With Vanderlip.
Capt. Eppingwell (Earnestly.)
Freda, do you know all the circumstances of this—er—affair? Do you know what you are doing?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: (Lightly.)....
You are asking questions, sir. It is not in the bond.
Capt. Eppingwell (Giving in.)
Right. I beg your pardon.

p.hi: (A knock is heard at street door. Doorkeeper opens. Enter messenger, an Indian, in parka and trail costume. He appears tired. He looks about hesitatingly, dazzled by the lights.)

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: (Recognizing messenger, to Freda.) Pardon me, please, a moment. I must speak to that man.
(Walks over to Indian.).
How soon she come?

div.head: INDIAN
div.p: Come soon. Much dogs. Come fast. One hour maybe. Maybe half-hour.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: All right. Come along.

p.hi: (Walks to Mrs. Eppingwell and Vanderlip at stove at right front, Indian at his heels.)

div.p: Here's that man I told you of, Maud. You had better speak with him—I beg your pardon, Vanderlip.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: That's all right. Business is business.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Oh, Mr. Vanderlip, I left my programme on the piano, and I really don't know with whom I have the next dance. Please.

p.hi: (She steps aside with Indian to talk.)
(Freda starts to cut off Vanderlip, crossing Capt. Eppingwell.)

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Oh, Freda! That waltz.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: One moment, please.

p.hi: (A dance has finished, and couples begin to stray in.)
(Clown and a lady accost Capt. Eppingwell, and the three move along together.)
(Mrs. McFee enters. As she passes by, she looks hard and suspiciously at Freda.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Come with me, Floyd. I want you now.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: And who are you, may I ask?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Freda.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: What the—
My God, Freda, what have you come here for?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: For you.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: I don't understand. You are nothing to me.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: And never have been anything, remember that, Floyd.
(Conveying the impression that she may be something to him in the immediate future.) But I want you now.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: And never will be anything, I assure you. (Getting back his courage.)
Faugh! What have you come here for, anyway?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: For you. And, moreover, you are going to come with me. You are going to let me take your arm, and you see that door there—you are going to take me out through it.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: I see myself doing it.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Yes, and I see you going on to my cabin.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: To your cabin?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Yes, to my cabin. I want to talk with you.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: This is a good place right here. Talk away.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: No, you must come with me.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Not on your life, Freda. Right here I stay.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: You have seen a little of me, Floyd; but you have heard more of me.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Oh, yes, I have heard that you play with men as a child plays with bubbles. It is a saying in the country. Well,
I am no bubble.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: What time is it, Floyd?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Twenty-five to twelve! Gee! I've got to get out of this!

p.hi: (Makes a hasty movement, as though to start toward street door. Freda takes his arm.)

div.p: What's this?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Nothing. Come along. I am in a hurry.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Now look here, Freda, I'm not going with you because you're making me. I've got to go anyway. I've got to be elsewhere, and pretty quick.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Oh, far from it. I never make anybody do anything. They just—do it.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: All right, I'll let you come with me, but only outside. I'm not going to your cabin.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: That is for you to determine. Let us start.

p.hi: (Mrs. Eppingwell talks with Indian. Mrs. Eppingwell now and again glances anxiously at Freda and Vanderlip; Mrs. McFee is more suspicious than ever, her hands involuntarily clutching and unclutching as though with desire to spring upon Freda and held back only by doubt.)

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: 'I'll have to rush. Got to change my clothes—

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Not for my cabin. Those clothes are good enough.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: But I tell you I am not going to your cabin.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Oh, well, never mind. The first thing is to get out of here. After that we'll see.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: You bet we'll see.

p.hi: (They start toward street door, Freda on his arm.)

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Who is that woman?

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: How should I know?

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Archie! I saw her lift her mask to you a moment ago.

div.head: CAPT. EPPINGWELL
div.p: I can't tell—I—she—

p.hi: (Mrs. Eppingwell does not listen further, but hastens to cut off Freda and Vanderlip.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: (Seeing Mrs. Eppingwell approaching.) If anybody stops me, Floyd, I shall quarrel, I know.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: For goodness' sake, don't make a scene.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Then get me out of here quick. Don't stop. (But Vanderlip stops when cut off by Mrs. Eppingwell.)

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: I beg pardon. You are not going, Mr. Vanderlip?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: I—yes, I'm going.
Mrs. Eppingwell But those dances?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: I've suddenly recollected something. I'm in a hurry. Please excuse me, Mrs. Eppingwell.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: And you promised to take me in to supper.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Of course, of course. And I will. I'll come back.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: I'd rather you didn't go—Floyd. The next dance
(Looking at his card.) is ours. It will begin in a minute.

p.hi: (Vanderlip does not know what to say. Freda urges him to continue toward door by tugging privily on his arm. Also she glances apprehensively at Mrs. McFee, who, with a set expression on face, has drawn nearer.)

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Really, Mrs. Eppingwell, I—

div.head: FREDA

p.hi: (Interrupting, urging him by arm to start toward door.)

div.p: We'll be late. We must go.

p.hi: (Vanderlip half starts to go with her toward door.)

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: I beg pardon, but you scarcely understand.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: It would be better, Mrs. Eppingwell, did your husband understand as well as I.

p.hi: (Mrs. Eppingwell is visibly hurt, and for the moment shocked into silence.)

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Now, look here, I'm not going to have any quarrelling between you women.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Who are you?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: One whose existence would scarcely interest you, Mrs. Eppingwell.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: (Whose efforts to make peace are ignored.) Oh, I say—

p.hi: (Mrs. McFee has drawn nearer. Everybody on stage is interested.)

div.p: Mrs. Eppingwell I have the right to know.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: As custodian of the community's morals?

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: And why not?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Ah, and why not?

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: You have the advantage. You know who I am. Who are you? I demand to know.
MRS. McFEE

p.hi: (Entering group with a very determined air and pausing an instant.)

div.p: We'll settle that, Mrs. Eppingwell.

p.hi: (Mrs. McFee suddenly springs upon Freda, tearing mask jrom face. Freda is startled and frightened. Vanderlip, the situation beyond him, stares helplessly back and forth between Freda and Mrs. Eppingwell. Everybody on the stage stares at Freda, forming a wide and irregular circle of onlookers, who are too polite to crowd closer, but who, nevertheless, cannot resist staring, one and all, from a distance.)

div.head: MRS. MCFEE
div.p: Mrs. Eppingwell, it is with great pleasure I make you acquainted with Freda Moloof—Miss Freda Moloof, as I understand.

p.hi: (Mrs. Eppingwell makes a gesture to silence Mrs. McFee, who pauses for a moment.)

div.p: Mayhap you dinna know the lady. Let me tell you—

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Now, here, I say, what's the good—
MRS. McFEE

p.hi: (Interrupting, and withering him with a look.)

div.p: Child of Perdition!
As I was saying, this woman's antecedents—a dancing girl, a destroyer of men's souls, a bold, brazen hussy, a servant of Satan, a—
Mrs. Eppingwell (Interrupting.)
That will do, Mrs. McFee. Will you please leave me to talk with her?

p.hi: (Mrs. McFee, still holding mask, snorts and withdraws a step from group.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: I do not want you to talk with me. What more can you say than that woman (Indicating Mrs. McFee, who snorts.) has said? I want to go. Come on, Floyd.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: I do not wish to be harsh.

div.head: FREDA

p.hi: (On verge oj tears, yet dry-eyed and resolute.)

div.p: Be anything but kind. That I will not bear.
Mrs. Eppingwell (Beginning gently.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: It is you that have the advantage now, hiding behind that mask. Your face is clothed. I am as naked before you, (Glancing around masked circle and shrinking as a naked woman might shrink.) before all of you.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: But you should not have come here.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: I had reason to come.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: An evil reason, I fear. However—

p.hi: (For a long moment they regard each other with fixed gaze, Freda aggressive, meteoric, at bay; Mrs. Eppingwell calm-eyed, serene, dispassionate. Freda begins to soften.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: You are kind.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: No; it is merely fair play.
MRS. McFEE
Why dinna you tell the hussy to go?

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Be quiet.

div.head: FREDA

p.hi: (Breaking down, seeming to droop for an instant, with one short dry sob or catch in the throat.)

div.p: Yes, I will go, Mrs. Eppingwell.
Will you come, Floyd?

p.hi: (Vanderlip looks to Mrs. Eppingwell for consent.)

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Mr. Vanderlip will stay.

p.hi: (Freda, broken down, beaten, but with no tears, no wringing of hands, nor customary signs of feminine weakness, with head up, mechanically resolute and defiant, ordinary carriage and speed of walk, goes toward street door. Silence. Everybody watches her. Doorkeeper does not assist her when she gropes blindly under bench for street moccasins.)
(What is emphasized is her isolation. She is not one of them, and they regard her as they would regard a strange animal which had strayed in out of the night.)

(She sits down on bench to put on street moccasins. Just as she lifts her foot to put on first moccasin, she pauses, thinks, then puts foot down again. She puts down moccasins, stands up, pauses irresolutely a moment, then walks forward to Mrs. Eppingwell and Vanderlip.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Mrs. Eppingwell, pardon me, but I had forgotten for the moment what I came for.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: And that is—?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Floyd Vanderlip.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Now look here, Freda, I tell you I won't stand for this.
Mrs. Eppingwell I trust, Miss Moloof—

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Call me Freda.
Everybody calls me Freda.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Well, Freda, then. Have you thought what you are doing? It is an awkward thing to play with souls. What right have you?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Right? I have no rights. Only privileges.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Licenses, I should say.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Thank you, licenses. I have licenses which you have not, for, you see, you are the wife of a captain.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: What do you want with this man?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: I might ask what you want with him? You have your husband.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: And you?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Men, just men.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: You are all that has been said of you, a destroyer of men.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Come on, Floyd. I want you. And be warned by Mrs. Eppingwell, I want to destroy you. (Imperiously.)
Come.

p.hi: (Vanderlip has by now been reduced to the helplessness of a puppet. He makes to start.)

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Floyd Vanderlip, you remain where you are. (He stops.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Come.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: (Warningly, imperiously.) Floyd!
MRS. McFEE

p.hi: (To Vanderlip, witheringly, imitating his hesitancy by bobbing her body.)

div.p: You weak and sinful creature, bobbing here, and bobbing there, like a chicken with its head cut off!

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Once for all, Freda, I'm not going with you.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: What time is it, Floyd?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Quarter to twelve! I must go, Mrs. Eppingwell. Good-by.

p.hi: (He starts toward door at heels of Freda, who leads him by a couple of steps.)

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Shame on you,

p.hi: (Freda glances back and smiles a hard smile.)

div.head: FREDA MOLOOF.
div.p: Floyd!

p.hi: (Vanderlip hesitates. Freda turns her face, blazingly imperious, upon him, and he slinks on after her. Dead silence.)

div.p: Help me on with my moccasins, Floyd.

p.hi: (He hesitates, with a last faint spark of rebellion. She looks at him, blazingly imperious.)

div.p: There they are.

p.hi: (He is beaten. Stoops for moccasins. She sits down on bench. He puts moccasins on her feet. They stand up. He helps her on with her cloak. While he is putting on his own moccasins and a big bearskin overcoat, she pulls hood of cloak over her head and covering her ears. Then she puts on her mittens. Then she waits for him. He puts on cap and mittens and opens street door.)

div.p: Go, get my mask.

p.hi: (He obeys, amid dead silence. Mrs. McFee mechanically surrenders mask to him. He returns. Opens door. Freda passes out. He follows.)

div.head: ACT III—FREDA MOLOOF'S CABIN
div.p: Scene. Freda Moloofs cabin. It is eleven forty-five at night. The room is large, and luxuriously furnished. Its walls are of logs stuffed between with brown moss. Doors of rough, unstained pine boards, also window-frames and sashes. Street door to rear, in centre. On either side of door is an ordinary, small-paned window. To left of door a plain chair. On rear wall, near door, are wooden pegs, from which hang cloaks, wraps, furs, etc., also wisp-brooms for brushing snow from moccasins.

The luxury of furnishing is of the solid order. No gim-cracks, no bric-a-brac. Furniture is rough, made in the Klondike. Tables, chairs, etc., are unpolished; they are made from pine lumber, are unstained, rough, massive. There is no carpet. Bearskins, etc., litter the floor. Strange juxtaposition of rough pine furniture, costly rugs, etc.; and, strangest of all, a grand piano. The cheapest and simplest and ugliest of kerosene lamps are used for lighting purposes, also candles. On walls are magnificent moose-horns and other appropriate trophies and weapons of the Northland (such as great ivory-headed spears and a pair of tusks of the mammoth); but there are no framed paintings.

p.hi: Midway between front and rear, and midway between centre and right, a large, wood-burning stove. Beside it a woodbox. On stove a tea-kettle is simmering. To left of stove, and near it, table, with table-cover on it, a few books and magazines, and a cheap kerosene lamp; around table several pine chairs. Between table and stove two easy chairs of rough pine, massive, thrown over with furs. On right, at front, against wall, a large, comfortable lounging-couch with many cushions. On left, at front, a grand piano. On piano a small, gilt French clock is ticking.

The room is luxurious, comfortable, picturesque, emphasizing the contact of civilization and the wilderness. In short, it is the best possible living apartment that money can purchase in the Klondike.

A Maid is in easy chair, reading magazine and yawning. Door opens on right. Indian enters with armful of firewood, which he carries to stove and dumps in woodbox. He proceeds to put several sticks of wood into stave and to adjust damper. His entrance arouses Maid, who looks up, yawns, lays magazine face-down on lap, yawns again, at same time stretching arms behind head, and glances at clock. It is quite a distance to clock. She rubs eyes and looks again.

div.head: MAID
div.p: Ten minutes to twelve. (Yawns.)

div.head: INDIAN
div.p: What time come?

div.head: MAID
div.p: I don't know.
I never know.

div.head: INDIAN
div.p: Me go to bed.

div.head: MAID
div.p: You'd better not. She said we were to stay up.

div.head: INDIAN
div.p: What for? Much trouble you think? What she do? Where she go?

div.head: MAID
div.p: How should I know?

div.head: INDIAN
div.p: Sitka Charley take dogs. Sitka Charley big hurry. What for?

div.head: MAID
div.p: There she comes now.

p.hi: (Maid rises to her feet, like a soldier coming to attention, hastily puts magazine on table, and brushes down front of skirt. Indian puts another stick of wood into stove and busies himself with raking ashes level in ash-box of stove.)
(Street door opens. Freda enters, leading Vanderlip by the hand. Both are mittened and in same wraps, coats, etc., with which they left anteroom of Pioneer Hall.)
(Indian finishes with stove and goes out slowly to right. Maid goes to rear and helps Freda off with wraps, moccasins, etc.)
(Vanderlip, who has come in reluctantly, does not remove mittens or cap, and stands sullenly inside the door, though he cannot forbear glancing curiously around.)

div.head: FREDA

p.hi: (Seeming in high spirits, while Maid is taking off her street moccasins.)

div.p: And now for a toddy! You've never tasted Minnie's. She makes them—
oh, to the king's taste, and to a Klondike king's at that.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Sorry. Won't have time. What did you want me for?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: My! There's the man of it!
(Imitating his voice and manner.) What did you want me for?
Can't let the poor woman catch her breath. Won't sit down for a moment in the warm.

p.hi: (Motions to Maid to help him off with his bearskin overcoat.)

div.p: Must know what he's wanted for. Must know right away. Must go right away. Oh, my! Oh, my!

p.hi: (Maid starts to help him off with overcoat. He jerks away from her.)

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: What do you want to say to me? Fire away.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Floyd—
—dear Floyd.... You are big and strong. I know, too, that you are kind. Be kind now, just a little kind, a very little. I can't talk with you here, this way. It would be ridiculous.

p.hi: (Beginning to help him take off coat, in which operation his assistance is restricted to non-resistance.)

div.p: Come and sit by the fire a moment.

p.hi: (Hands overcoat to Maid, who hangs it up on wall.)

div.p: Just for a moment.

p.hi: (Untying ear-flaps, and removing his cap, which Maid hangs up. She pushes him on to chair and lifts one foot to remove street moccasins.)

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Now here, I say—
I won't have a woman doing that for me.

p.hi: (Pushes her away and removes moccasins himself. He stands up.)

div.p: I said I wasn't coming to your cabin, Freda; and I can't stay anyway—only for that one moment, that's all.

div.head: FREDA

p.hi: (Taking his hand and starting to lead him forward.)

div.p: That is all I wanted, just the moment. And it is sweet of you to give it to me.

p.hi: (Vanderlip pauses and looks around room with interest. Freda pauses with him. Maid remains in rear, putting moccasins away, etc.)

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: I say, Freda, you're fixed comfortably.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Think so?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: It's grand style, I must say. Nothing like it in the land. You're the only person that has three rooms.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Four—counting the kitchen.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: And my cabin is one room.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: And you a millionaire.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: But this is the Klondike—

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Where even millionaires
(Imitating Dave Harney.) can't buy sweetenin' for their coffee an' mush. Dodgast the luck anyway.

p.hi: (Vanderlip laughs appreciatively. They start on again to front, but he sees piano and stops again.)

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: If there ain't a piano! It cost you a pretty penny, I'll bet.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: "You cannot pack a Broadwood half a mile." (Looking at him.)
Don't you know it?
Don't know your Kipling!
Here's the way it goes—

lg.l: "You couldn't pack a Broadwood half a mile,
You mustn't leave a fiddle in the damp,
You couldn't raft an organ up the Nile
And play it in an equatorial swamp "——

div.head: VANDERLIP

p.hi: (Who had first gazed admiringly at her, then gazed curiously around until, by clock on piano, he sees what time it is, interrupting by bringing hand heavily down on keys of piano.)

div.p: I can't wait another second. What do you want with me?

div.head: FREDA

p.hi: (Ceasing the song, looking up quite calmly, and placing hand over face of clock.)

div.p: I want you to stop looking at that clock. And

p.hi: (Rising, taking him by hand, and leading him toward stove.)

div.p: I want you to come right over here and be good.
Minnie.

p.hi: (Maid, who has been waiting in rear, comes forward and again waits.)

(Freda pushes Vanderlip into easy chair near stove, runs to couch at right for cushion, which she puts behind his head, pressing his shoulders and head back upon it. She places fur-covered footstool under his feet. He has not relaxed himself, and in his stiff acceptance of comforts makes a ridiculous appearance.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: (Giving cushion behind head a last pat.) And now you may smoke.

p.hi: (Vanderlip rolls head back and forth on cushion. His hand searches for watch, which he draws forth from pocket. But before he can look at it Freda's hand covers the face of it.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Oh my! My! What a busy man it is!

p.hi: (Maid enters with cigar-box on tray. Vanderlip takes a cigar, and while he examines it critically Freda puts watch back in his pocket.)

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Real Havana. And you can't buy them for love nor money. How do you manage it?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: (Striking match and holding it up to him.) Oh, I just do. I could have offered you worse, I assure you.

p.hi: (Vanderlip puffs on cigar—long, slow, appreciative puffs. His face loses its sullen expression. He sighs contentedly. He relaxes his body, sinks back, and for the first time looks really comfortable.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: And now, Minnie, you have your reputation to live up to.

div.head: MAID
div.p: The Scotch?

p.hi: (Freda nods head, and Maid goes out to right.)

div.head: VANDERLIP

p.hi: (Taking cigar from mouth and looking at it.)

div.p: I say, Freda, you can make a fellow comfortable.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Think so?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: (The sullenness returning into his face.) And you know how to make him uncomfortable.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Think so?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: You are, by long odds, the most brutal woman I ever met.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: (Incredulously and innocently aghast.) I?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: I wouldn't treat a dog the way you treated me. (Growing angry.)
You treated me like a cur, the way you lugged me away from the dance.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Think so?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: I'd sooner a man beat me with a club, than take what I took from you. It was just as much as if you took a club to me. You beat me into submission, in front of everybody, until I followed at your heels—that's what you did.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: But you are not the Lord. You are Freda—Freda
And whom Freda chasteneth—

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: She—

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Not at all. The Lord is the Lord, but Freda is only a woman....

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: And?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Her ways are different from the Lord's.

p.hi: (She pulls her chair alongside of his, and rests one hand for a moment, caressingly, on his. Speaks softly.)

div.p: And aren't you glad?

p.hi: (The caress has its effect. He is soothed, and puffs away at cigar with half-closed eyes.)
(Freda, unobserved, throws a swift glance at clock, listens intently as for sounds from without of an approaching sled, and betrays to her audience her anxiety and restlessness.)
(Maid enters with two glasses on a tray. Freda, observed by Vanderlip, sips from one glass, nods head approvingly, and passes it to him. Takes other glass herself.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Minnie. Candles.

p.hi: (Maid moves about room, putting out lamps and lighting candles, which latter, with tissue-paper shades, shed softer light.)
(Vanderlip suddenly recollects himself and draws watch. Freda tries to cover watch with hand, but jails. Vanderlip sees watch and starts to rise from chair. Freda half rises and presses him back.)

div.head: VANDERLIP

p.hi: (With note of real regret in his voice, glancing from cigar in one hand, and glass in other hand, to the stove, about the room, and then at Freda.)

div.p: It's a darn shame to leave all this, but I've really got to, Freda. I don't think I was ever so comfortable in my life.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Then why leave it, Floyd?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: I've got to hit the trail to-night, right away. And I've got to get my trail clothes. That bearskin overcoat's too warm. Can't travel in it.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Wait a minute. Let me think.
(Thinks a moment. Her face brightens.) Ah, the very thing. Why not send my Indian for your things? He can bring them here. That will give you a few minutes more of the warm—

div.head: VANDERLIP

p.hi: (Interrupting, putting his arm out and around her waist.)

div.p: And of you, Freda.

p.hi: (Freda lets his arm linger for a moment, then, warning him, by a look, of presence of Maid, gently disengages arm. Takes her time about disengaging it. Vanderlip sinks back comfortably on cushion.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Minnie.

p.hi: (Maid, who has finished lighting candles, approaches.)

div.p: Send Joe here. Tell him to put on his mittens and parka.

p.hi: (Freda resumes seat, and lays one hand on Vanderlip's hand. Neither speaks.)
(Maid enters, followed by Indian, who, as he comes, is putting on parka and mittens.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: You know Mr. Vanderlip's cabin?

div.head: INDIAN
div.p: Um.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Give him the key, Floyd.

p.hi: (Vanderlip reaches in pocket and gives key to Indian.)

div.p: You go Mr. Vanderlip's cabin and get parka—

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Dog-whip, fur cap, all together with parka.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Dog-whip, fur cap, all together with parka. (Indian nods.)

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: And flask of whiskey on table.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: And flask of whiskey on table.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: And go quick.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: And go quick.

p.hi: (Indian nods and starts toward door to rear. Makes exit. Freda rises, as though recollecting something.)

div.p: Excuse me, Floyd.

(Passes behind Vanderlip's back toward door to right, and unobserved beckons Maid. They pause at door to right.) Run quick, out the kitchen door, and catch Joe. Tell him not to come back. Tell him I said so—to go get drunk, anything, but not to come back.

p.hi: (Vanderlip lifts heady turns head around, and is watching and listening. Freda continues in slightly louder voice.)

div.p: And then, Cupid's stew.

p.hi: (Freda returns to chair, passing hand caressingly through Vanderlip's hair before she sits down.)

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: What were you gassing about?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Cupid's stew.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: I heard it, but what is it?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Well, first you take the chafing-dish—

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: What's the chafing-dish? Use them in churches, don't they? Burn incense in them, or something or other.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: A chafing-dish, silly, is a very pretty something you cook things in.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Oh, I see. A highfalutin' frying-pan.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: First you put some butter in it; and then, when the butter is melted, you stir in—oh, say a tablespoon of flour.
When it is stirred smooth—

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Do you brown the flour?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: No, of course not.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Oh.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Then you stir in a cup of milk—Minnie's fixing it now, out in the kitchen—and in her case it will have to be condensed milk—

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: St. Anthony's Cream's the best brand I know of.
But you can't get it in this country.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: I've got some.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: No!

div.head: FREDA
div.p: I have. Then you put in some boneless chicken—tinned—

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: You got some of that, too?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Yes. And then some mushrooms—tinned—

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Freda, you're a wonder!

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Then season to taste,
(Rising to climax.) and there you are!

p.hi: (Freda half rises, leaning toward him. He half rises to meet her, reaching for her with both arms, to put around her waist, but she catches his hands and very gently and slowly disengages herself. Her very manner of disengaging herself is caressing and seducing. They sink back slowly into their respective chairs.)
(Freda listens intently, as for the sound of a sled without. Glances anxiously at clock on piano. Vanderlip does not notice, for he is drawing his watch and looking at it.)

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: It's ten after twelve.
Gee! I hate to go without having a crack at that Cupid's stew.

p.hi: (He looks at Freda. She is gazing at him absently, apparently lost in meditation over him.)

div.p: Well?

div.head: FREDA

p.hi: (Startled, as though discovered, in pretty embarrassment.)

div.p: Oh!

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: I was just wondering what you wanted to see me about.
(He draws his chair snugly against hers. She looks at him, studying him, as though trying to make up her mind to speak.) Well, what is it?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Floyd, I am tired of the whole business. I want to go away—over the ice—anywhere—away. I can't live it out here till the river breaks next spring. I'll die. I know it. I want to quit it all and go away. And I want to go at once.

p.hi: (She lays her hand in appeal on the back of his. His hand turns over and captures hers. He does not know what to say.)

div.p: Well?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: I don't know what to say. Nothing I'd like better, Freda. You know that well enough.

p.hi: (He presses her hand, and she nods.)

div.p: But you see I'm—
—I'm engaged. Of course you know that. Everybody knows it. The girl's coming in over the ice to marry me.
Don't know what was up with me when I asked her, but it was a long while back, and I was all-fired young.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: And you intend to wait for her?
And to marry her?
Men sometimes make mistakes, you know, when they are young.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: And this is one of them. What did I know about women then?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Nothing to what you know about them now.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: I should say so.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: But, Floyd, by persisting in the mistake, do you mend matters?
Will you be happy? Will she be happy? She is sure to find out the mistake, then it will be tragedy.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: I don't know. Women keep bothering me so. There are so many of them, and I like them all. Seems to me I like best the one I'm with at the time.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Mrs. Eppingwell, let us say.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Yes, Mrs. Eppingwell. Why, when I'm with her, I think there's nothing like her under the sun. I feel like going out and killing her husband just to get her.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: And when you are with me, Floyd?

p.hi: (Vanderlip reaches out impulsively and draws her to him. Her head rests on his shoulder. She snuggles in to him in a contented way, her hand petting his. He buries his face in her hair. The scent of her hair gets into his brain and maddens him. He disengages hand from hers and slips it gradually up her bare arm. His other arm, about waist and shoulder, draws her closely against him. All the while, however, they are occupying their respective chairs. They remain this way for a long moment or so, his hand still progressing up her bare arm.)

div.head: FREDA

p.hi: (Tearing herself suddenly loose from him and holding him from her at arms' length, tragically.)

div.p: Floyd! Floyd! I want to go away—out of the land—anywhere!—anywhere!

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Dear Freda.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: I am tired, tired, so tired of it all. I—I—
—I think I shall cry.

div.head: VANDERLIP

p.hi: (Gently and soothingly drawing her to him.)

div.p: There, there, little woman. Brace up, buck up, don't give in.

div.head: FREDA

p.hi: (Slowly disengaging herself and gently holding him off at arm's length.)

div.p: I've been running over in my mind the men I know, and reached the conclusion that... that...

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: I was the likeliest of the lot.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: No, not that, but... but... that I liked you best of all.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Dear Freda.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Dear Floyd.

p.hi: (Door on right opens. They break away from each other and assume a more decorous position. Maid enters, bearing tray, on which are chafing-dish, dishes, napkins, etc., and a quart bottle of champagne. She sets tray on table. Freda serves Cupid's stew to Vanderlip, while Maid, a little to rear, is wrestling with champagne bottle.)

div.head: VANDERLIP

p.hi: (Who has not noticed champagne bottle, aroused by popping of cork and turning around quickly, simulating a person roused from sleep, rubbing his eyes, etc.)

div.p: Wake me up, somebody. I'm dreaming. Pinch me.

p.hi: (Takes hold of bottle, Maid still retaining her hold, and looks at it.)

div.p: The real thing.

p.hi: (Releases bottle and looks admiringly at Freda.)

div.p: Freda, you're a peach. There isn't another bottle in the Klondike.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Oh, yes, there is.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: You've got to show me.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: I've three dozen in the store-room—(Turning to Maid.)
Isn't that right, Minnie?

div.head: MAID
div.p: And two over. I counted them this afternoon.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Gosh!

div.head: FREDA
div.p: All right, Minnie. You may go now.

p.hi: (Vanderlip begins eating Cupid's stew. Shows that he is pleased with it. Freda watches him, herself eating. Glances at clock, and listens. She seems to hear something. Puts down her plate on table. A knock is heard on door at rear. Freda rises, goes swiftly to rear, and opens door.)
(An Indian enters. He is dazzled by the light, and pulls ice from lips. Freda shuts door. Vanderlip, after one glance around, goes on eating and drinking.)

div.head: INDIAN
div.p: Hello.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: (Not knowing his errand.) Hello.

div.head: INDIAN
div.p: Brrr! Much cold.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Very cold.

div.head: INDIAN
div.p: Me come Sitka Charley.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Oh, you are the man.

div.head: INDIAN
div.p: Sitka Charley say him come quick.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: How quick?

div.head: INDIAN
div.p: Maybe ten minutes. What time now?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Fifteen minutes after twelve.

div.head: INDIAN
div.p: Him come twenty-five minutes after twelve. Ten minutes more him come, I think.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: How is the girl?

div.head: INDIAN
div.p: Much tired. Ride on sled. Plenty tired, cry little bit, like baby. She say must camp right away. Sitka Charley say make Dawson. She say no camp right away she die. Sitka Charley say don't care, make Dawson anyway. I go now. Good-by.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Don't you want to go out in the kitchen and get warm?

div.head: INDIAN
div.p: No. Good-by.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Good-by.
You haven't told me how you like it.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: (Turning plate upside down.) Actions speak louder than words. (She helps him to some more.) Let me see, Cupid's slumgullion, eh?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Cupid's stew.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: (Thrusting fork into stew on his plate.) What's in a name, so long as it's in your plate anyway?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Floyd.
Floyd.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: (Looking at her.) Unh-hunh.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: I've been thinking. Why couldn't we go down river?

div.head: VANDERLIP

p.hi: (Dropping fork and looking at her blankly, then around room, then at plate, and holding up glass of champagne—pathetically.)

div.p: And leave all this?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Why not? We'd soon be down in the world, where we could swim in wine and all kinds of good things.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: I don't know, Freda. I almost believe you've got to be in a place like this to get the value out of things. I tell you champagne on tap is not all it's cracked up to be. It never bites in and lays hold the way this does. Down in the world it's all wine and no thirst—

div.head: FREDA
div.p: And up here it's all thirst and no wine.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: But when you do get hold of the wine—Lord! Lord!

(Tilts hack head and empties glass, his face beaming like to the full moon. He regards Freda thoughtfully as she fills his glass, and speaks with sudden suspicion.) You don't happen to care for palaces, do you?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Why, what put that into your head?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Well, I had a hankering after them myself, till I got to thinking a while back, and I've about sized it up that one gets fat living in palaces, and soft and lazy. No sir, no champagne on tap and soft summer skies for me.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: I suppose it's nice in palaces—for a time. But one would soon tire. The world is good, but life should be many-sided. The way we'll do it will be to rough and knock about for a while, and then rest up somewhere.
Off to the South Seas on a yacht, then, say a nibble of Paris.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Paris!

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Then a winter in South America, and a summer in Norway—

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: I always wanted a look-see, at South America.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: A few months in England—

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Good society?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Certainly. And then, heigho! for the dogs and the sleds and the Hudson Bay Country!

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Freda, you were made for me! It's just the life I want. I couldn't have hit it off better myself if I'd tried. The way you put it—a bit of this, and a bit of that—variety, you know—that's me.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: That's it, variety, change. A strong man like you, full of vitality and go, could not possibly stand a palace for a year.
It's all very well for effeminate men, but you weren't made for such a life. You are masculine, intensely masculine.

div.head: VANDERLIP

p.hi: (Taking her hand and beginning to draw her toward him.)

div.p: Do you think so?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: It doesn't require thinking. I know. Have you ever noticed that it was easy to make women care for you?

div.head: VANDERLIP

p.hi: (Superbly innocent, yet showing by his expression that he agrees with her.)

div.p: Oh, I don't know.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: You know it is so.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Well, for the sake of argument, yes.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: It is very easy. And why?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Darned if I know.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Because you are masculine. You strike the deepest chords of a woman's heart. Woman is weak. You are a wall of strength to her. You are something to cling to—big-muscled, strong, and brave. In short, because you are a man.
Dear, dear Floyd!

p.hi: (She lies in his arms a long moment, both still on their respective chairs. Then she slowly and gently disengages herself, at the same time stealing a glance at the clock.)

div.head: VANDERLIP

p.hi: (Holding up her arm and studying it for a moment.)

div.p: How much do you weigh, Freda?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: What now?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: I just wanted to know.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: But why?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Oh, nothing, I was just thinking you were not the kind to put on fat?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: (Decisively.) Well, I think not!

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: (Suddenly, by her hands, lifts her to her feet and thrusts her several steps away from him, then, sinking back in chair and running his eyes critically over her) Your lines are good.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Think so?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: You just bet I do.
You'll never get fat!

div.head: FREDA

p.hi: (Coming to his chair and rumpling his hair.)

div.p: No, thank goodness, I wasn't born that way.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Now some women—

div.head: FREDA
div.p: The Lisznayi, for example.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: She'll never get fat, Freda.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Oh, she won't, eh? How do you know? You'd never have guessed it all of yourself. She must have told you.
Why, she's started already. She's carrying twenty pounds more than she ought. It spoils her figure. And—my!—now that she's started, won't she just put it on!

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: But how do you know?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: I've my eyes. So have you. Surely you've noticed it?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Honest, now, I've had my suspicions that way. (He remains silent for a moment or so. Freda rumples his hair.)
I like that.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: What?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: That what you are doing.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Oh!

p.hi: (Slaps his arm playfully, and sits down in her chair. Listens intently for sounds from without, while Vanderlip sips from glass.)

div.head: VANDERLIP

p.hi: (After a pause, setting down glass and looking amorously at Freda.)

div.p: Say, Freda, do you know...
Do you know what I'd like?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Not in the slightest.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Well, I'll tell you. I'd like to see you with your hair down.

div.head: FREDA

p.hi: (Change in whole manner beginning here, but beginning slightly.)

div.p: Think so?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: You just bet I would.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Wait a moment.

p.hi: (Passes behind him to door at right.)
(Vanderlip rests under the idea that she has gone to take down hair, fills glass, and leans complacently back in chair and sips from glass.)
(Freda opens door to right and beckons. Closes door, listens for a moment on way back to chair, and sits down.)

div.head: VANDERLIP

p.hi: (Looking at her hair, still up, surprised and grieved.)

div.p: Why, I thought all the time you were taking it down.

p.hi: (Freda laughs her silvery, scornful laughter. Vanderlip is puzzled, thinks she is teasing him.)

(Maid enters, unobserved by Vanderlip. Freda issues her order with her eyes, glancing at Vanderlip's bearskin overcoat hanging on wall to rear. Maid goes and gets coat and returns, still unobserved by Vanderlip, at the rear of whom she stands waiting.)

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Now I say, Freda.
What's the matter anyway?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: I have just recollected.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: What?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: That you had an engagement at twelve sharp.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: I did. But it will keep.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: It is now half-past twelve.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Well, and what of it?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Nothing, only...

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Only what?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Only, isn't it rather cold down at the water-hole?

p.hi: (Vanderlip is stunned jor a moment, and can only stare at her in a bewildered way.)
(Her laughter, at his bewilderment, becomes wholly mirthful.)

div.p: Minnie, help Mr. Vanderlip on with his overcoat.

p.hi: (Vanderlip glances swiftly around and sees Maid holding coat. He looks at his watch very slowly, and puts it away very slowly. Slowly empties glass of champagne, and carefully puts empty glass on table. Just as slowly drags himself out of chair and to his feet. Maid offers to help on with overcoat, but he ignores her.)

div.head: FREDA

p.hi: (Who has ceased laughing, showing that she is a bit frightened by his preternatural calmness, but still keeping her nerve.)

div.p: Let me thank you for your kindness, Floyd. I wanted half an hour or so of your time, and you have given it. The turning to the left, as you leave the cabin, leads quickest to the water-hole. Good-night. I'm going to bed.

p.hi: (Starts to go toward door at left.)

div.p: Minnie, see Mr. Vanderlip out, please.

p.hi: (Turning head over shoulder, looking back at Vanderlip, and beginning again her silvery laughter. Vanderlip has not spoken a word. He springs, lionlike, after her, seizing her by the arm and whirling her fiercely about, face to face, and still keeping his clutch.)

div.p: Don't be rough.

p.hi: (He glares at her. She still keeps her nerve, speaks lightly.)

div.p: On second thought—
—I've decided not to go to bed. Don't be ridiculous, Floyd.
Tragedy doesn't at all become you. Do sit down and be comfortable.

p.hi: (To Maid, who has remained composed and holding coat.)

div.p: Mr. Vanderlip doesn't want his coat yet awhile. (Maid goes to rear, hangs up coat, and remains at rear, waiting.)

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: (Speaking with slow, clear enunciation.) What do you know about the water-hole?

p.hi: (Freda laughs. He closes his grip on her arm till she winces.)

div.p: What do you know about the water-hole?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: More than you know.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Then tell me. I want to know.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: I know that the fair lady waiting there has flown away a good half-hour ago.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Where?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Down the river.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: How do you know it?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: I arranged it.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Tell me, it was because you wanted me?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: No.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: (Hardening again.) Then you didn't want me? (She shakes her head.)
You don't want me?
Well, then, will you have me?—Now? (She shakes head.)
Then this was a game you worked on me?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Yes.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: You didn't mean a word of it?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Not a word of it. I was playing.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Well, I wasn't, that's the difference.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Do let go of my arm. You are hurting me.

div.head: VANDERLIP

p.hi: (Ignoring her protest, dragging her roughly by her arm to the front and just to left of table, holding her face to face with him, and beginning to speak faster.)

div.p: Look here, Freda, I'm a fool. I know it. I was a fool there in that chair. You put it all over me. You women all make a fool of me. I don't think quick. I'm not used to it, I guess. My tongue is awkward. I can't think of bright things to say, or the right things to say. And I believe what is said to me. And then I like women, too. I can't help it. I was born that way. I just like them, and they take advantage of me—

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Won't you let go of me and sit down?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Why do they take advantage of me?

Because I am a fool. Because I am playing their game and don't know how to play it. They know how to play it. They ought to know—it is their game. A man's a fool to buck another man's game. The percentage is all in favor of the house. And a man is a bigger fool to buck a woman's game. And I've been dead soft and easy. I know it. I've played your game and you've tied knots in me...

p.hi: (He pauses, as though debating the next thing to say.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: I must say you are untying the knots fast.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: I'm untying nothing. I'm going to begin tying. What I'm going to do is to play my game, and you're going to play it with me, my lady.
(His speech grows slow and clear again.) Do you know what my game is?
It's not palavering, and being society-monkey, and ducking, and bowing, and scraping, and giving crooked talk, and saying smart things, and that sort of stuff. It's just this—

p.hi: (He takes hold of her other arm with other hand, and puts the pressure on with both hands. At first she merely winces but he grips until she cries aloud in pain. Maid shows alarm for first time, and starts hastily forward.)

div.p: That's it. Muscle's my game—the only game I can play, and I've been a fool to go out of my class.

div.head: MAID
div.p: What shall I do?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Nothing. It is all right.

div.head: MAID
div.p: Shall I go for help?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: No, no.
Let go of me, Floyd. You are crushing my arms.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Did you let go when you crushed me?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: You coward!

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Were you less coward when you beat me down to my knees with your woman's wit, your woman's beauty, your woman's weapons? Your face is beautiful. Your body is beautiful. With these have you drawn me to you, making yourself soft and yielding, so that at a distance the very feel of you was soft and yielding—

—a play actress, you! Your mind is quick. Your tongue is crooked. You lied to me. When you let me hold your hand, you lied to me. When you looked softly at me, or passed your hand through my hair, you lied to me. When you came against me and rested your head on my breast so that the scent of your hair got into my brain and maddened me, you lied to me. You knew all the time that my blood was pounding up hot within me, you knew all the time that I was honest and playing fair, and all the time you were lying to me.

p.hi: (He pauses and debates upon what next to say.)

div.head: MAID
div.p: Shall I go for help?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Shut up, you!

Well, I've taken your medicine. Now you take mine. Here it is. I want you. I'm pretty sure I'd sooner have you than Loraine. You can marry me if you want, but marry or no marry, you're mine. Down river you go with me tonight, my lady, so you'd better tell that girl of yours to pack your duds.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Think so?

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: I know so—and here's a foretaste of my game. Tell me how you like it.

p.hi: (Bends her back, face upturned, gets proper grips so that she is helpless, and deliberately and passionately kisses her several times on the lips. Maid springs upon him, but he flings her off and away with one arm. Holds Freda by one arm again.)

div.p: How do you like it, eh? How do you like it?

div.head: FREDA

p.hi: (Almost suffocating with rage, wiping lips with back of free hand.)

div.p: You beast! You beast! You beast!
(Maid is starting to spring at him again.) No, no, Minnie! Stop! I can deal with him.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Not in a man's game, Freda.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: In a man's game, Floyd Vanderlip.

p.hi: (She no longer winces nor struggles to free herself, but confronts him, head erect, expression of cold anger on face.)

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: (Looking at her admiringly for a moment.) Ah, you beauty! You've made me mad for you. I'll crush you into submission as you crushed me into submission at the dance to-night. You beat me down to my knees, but I'll bring you down on your knees to me till you're glad to kiss the toe of my moccasin.
And now, you beauty, you beauty, I am thirsty for your lips again.

p.hi: (He starts to bend her back again, but she revises to struggle, holding her face up to him defiantly. He pauses.)

div.p: Well, why don't you fight and scratch and claw around some?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Because I won't give you the chance to pull and haul and maul me around, that is all.

div.head: VANDERLIP

p.hi: (Who, as usual, is baffled by a change of attitude.)

div.p: Then I'll kiss you.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: You may pollute me with your lips, but you shall not master me with your strength.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Nay, nay, not pollute. You should call it (Imitating Mrs. McFee.) "contameenate." That's right. Blaze away at me with those eyes of yours. You may keep quiet with your body, but you can't take the fight out of your eyes. I tell you that blaze gives value to your kisses, and now I'm going to—

p.hi: (Leans forward to kiss her, while she remains motionless and passive. He pauses, with lips close to hers.)

div.p: Nothing like prolonging anticipation, eh? You know you said I was masculine, intensely masculine. How do you like it? How do you like leaning up against the wall of my strength? Ah, you beauty! You beauty!

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Minnie! Open the door!

p.hi: (A jingling of dog bells is heard without, and a man's voice crying "Haw!" Maid runs toward the door. Vanderlip listens, still holding Freda close in his arms. A knock at door. Maid throws open door.)

div.head: FREDA

p.hi: (In triumphant voice, as door is thrown open.)

div.p: Now will you let go of me?

p.hi: (Enter Mrs. Eppingwell, followed by Capt. Eppingwell and a Northwest mounted Policeman.)
(Mrs. Eppingwell, looking at Policeman, points at Vanderlip.)
(Policeman hesitates, embarrassed at interrupting such a scene.)

(Vanderlip and Freda in consternation, he still holding her. He releases her abruptly and is himself all awkwardness and confusion. Freda separates from him, moving away unconsciously several steps, her eyes fixed upon Mrs. Eppingwell.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: You!

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Yes, I. And I am glad I am not too late.

div.head: FREDA

p.hi: (Striving to recover her poise, speaking automatically in artificial manner.)

div.p: Delighted, I assure you.

p.hi: (With sudden break in manner, becoming candid.)

div.p: No, I am not delighted at all.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: I should scarcely think so.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: It is intrusion.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: It is intrusion, I know, but—

div.head: FREDA
div.p: (Interrupting, again artificial manner.) Oh, not at all.
(Starting toward Mrs. Eppingwell.) Won't you take off your wraps?
Minnie!

p.hi: (Maid offers to help Mrs. Eppingwell off with wraps.)

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: No, it is not necessary. We shall stop only a moment.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: I hope you'll pardon my curiosity, but—(Hesitates an instant.) —why didn't you come sooner? What was the delay?

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: I had to get this gentleman. It took time—

div.head: POLICEMAN
div.p: Sorry.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: And then I went to the wrong water-hole.

p.hi: (Freda and Vanderlip both start, Mrs. Eppingwell observing Vanderlip's start.)

div.p: Good morning, Mr. Vanderlip.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Hum, yes. How do you do? Good morning.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: (The real state of affairs dawning on her.) I see. You expected to find me at the water-hole.
And you didn't.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: No. Then I went to the other water-hole.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Expecting to find me?

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Yes. Then I came here.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Unerring instinct.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Yes, wasn't it?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Er—by the way, didn't you find anybody at the second water-hole?

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: A strange woman. I thought she was you at first. She seemed restless enough.

div.head: VANDERLIP

p.hi: (Starts at mention of strange woman, suddenly moving toward the street door.)

div.p: I've fooled around here long enough. I'm going.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Good luck, Floyd.

div.head: POLICEMAN
div.p: Sorry.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: What's the matter now?

div.head: POLICEMAN
div.p: I've got a warrant for you. Forgery. Sorry.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: What in hell—

div.head: POLICEMAN
div.p: Sorry.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Now look here, I say, whose game is this?

p.hi: (Freda laughs her silvery laughter, it is laughter of amusement only.)

div.head: FREDA
div.p: You did this.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: I had tried everything else to stop him from running away.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: (Laughing merrily and shaking her head.) Poor Floyd! Poor, poor Floyd!

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Look here, Mrs. Eppingwell. This is your work. You'd better call it off. I'm done with bucking other people's games.

p.hi: (Starts toward door, but Policeman lays hand on his arm.)

div.p: Get out of my way, you whipper-snapper!

div.head: POLICEMAN
div.p: Sorry.

div.head: VANDERLIP

p.hi: (Flinging off hand, but remaining where he is.)

div.p: You'd better call him off, Mrs. Eppingwell, or there'll be the almightiest ruction round here you ever saw.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Don't be in a hurry, Floyd. She's gone.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: No, she isn't.

div.head: FREDA
div.p: Ask Mrs. Eppingwell.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Whom do you mean?

div.head: FREDA
div.p: The strange, restless lady at the water-hole.

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: Why, yes. She went away on a sled down the river.

div.head: VANDERLIP
div.p: Who'd she go with?

div.head: MRS. EPPINGWELL
div.p: With nobody. She had an Indian dog-driver, though.
